sites.s: Nabataean tomb city · World Heritage
sites.te: The southern city of the Nabataeans
sites.se: 111 tombs carved into sandstone outcrops, with dated inscriptions from 1 BC to AD 74
sites.sa: 111 مقبرة منحوتة في نتوءات الحجر الرملي، بنقوش مؤرخة من 1 ق.م إلى 74 م
sites.desc: The largest Nabataean site south of Petra: 111 monumental tombs cut into sandstone outcrops around a now-vanished city, 94 of them decorated, with dated inscriptions running from 1 BC to AD 74. Qasr al-Bint, the largest, is about 16 m high. Water came from wells and cisterns in the plain. Rome annexed the Nabataean kingdom in AD 106 and a Roman garrison is attested at Hegra. Inscribed in 2008 as Saudi Arabia's first World Heritage site; excavated by the Saudi-French Madâ'in Sâlih Archaeological Project since 2008.
sites.sig: The best-preserved Nabataean tombs anywhere, and the only ones with a run of dated inscriptions.
sites.ex: Saudi-French Madâ’in Sâlih Archaeological Project (L. Nehmé) 2008 onwards; Royal Commission for AlUla
disc: Tombs dated by inscription from 1 BC to AD 74
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre. Hegra Archaeological Site (al-Hijr / Madā ͐ in Ṣāliḥ) (ref. 1293), inscribed 2008.

sites.s: Neolithic stone monuments · AlUla–Khaybar
sites.te: A thousand rectangles in the desert
sites.se: Stone enclosures up to 620 m long, built 7,000 years ago and holding cattle horns as offerings
sites.sa: حظائر حجرية يصل طولها إلى 620 م، بُنيت قبل 7,000 عام وتضم قرون ماشية كقرابين
sites.desc: Long rectangular stone structures, 20 to 620 m in length, found by the thousand across north-west Arabia from the Nafud to the lava fields of Khaybar: more than 1,000 are recorded over about 200,000 km². Excavation of a mustatil near AlUla found a chamber with cattle, sheep and gazelle horns placed as offerings around a standing stone, radiocarbon-dated to about 5300–5000 BC, making them among the oldest large-scale monuments in the world. Their builders were cattle herders of a wetter Arabia.
sites.sig: Older than the pyramids and Stonehenge, and until 2021 almost unknown outside Arabia.
sites.ex: Aerial Archaeology in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (University of Western Australia) and Royal Commission for AlUla, 2018 onwards
disc: Cattle horns deposited around a standing stone
refs: Thomas, H., Kennedy, M. A., Dalton, M. et al. (2021). The mustatils: cult and monumentality in Neolithic north-western Arabia. Antiquity 95(381), 605–626.
Kennedy, M. A. et al. (2023). Cult, herding and pilgrimage in the Late Neolithic of north-west Arabia. PLOS ONE 18(3).

sites.s: Najdi mud-brick capital · World Heritage
sites.el: Salwa Palace and mud-brick city on Wadi Hanifah
sites.te: A capital made of earth
sites.se: The mud-brick heart of the First Saudi State, on a bend of Wadi Hanifah
sites.sa: قلب الدولة السعودية الأولى من الطوب الطيني، على منعطف وادي حنيفة
sites.desc: A walled district of mud brick on the edge of Wadi Hanifah, settled in the 15th century and from 1727 the capital of the First Saudi State until an Ottoman-Egyptian siege took it in 1818. Salwa Palace, the Imam Mohammed bin Saud Mosque and houses of the Najdi style, with thick adobe walls, triangular openings and tamarisk roofs, survive. Inscribed in 2010 under criteria (iv), (v) and (vi) and restored as part of the Diriyah project.
sites.sig: The finest surviving example of Najdi architecture and the birthplace of the Saudi state.
sites.ex: Diriyah Gate Development Authority; Saudi Commission for Tourism and National Heritage
disc: Najdi mud-brick style with triangular vents
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre. At-Turaif District in ad-Dir’iyah (ref. 1329), inscribed 2010.

sites.s: Largest oasis in the world · World Heritage
sites.te: Two and a half million palms
sites.se: Springs feed the largest oasis on Earth, farmed without a break since the Neolithic
sites.sa: عيون تغذي أكبر واحة على الأرض، زُرعت دون انقطاع منذ العصر الحجري الحديث
sites.desc: An oasis of about 85.4 km² in the Eastern Province with some 2.5 million date palms watered by more than 280 artesian springs from the Neogene aquifer. Twelve components, including gardens, canals, springs, Jawatha mosque and Qasr Ibrahim, record settlement from the Neolithic to the present. Inscribed in 2018 under criteria (iii), (iv) and (v) as the world's largest oasis.
sites.sig: A cultural landscape that shows how people have farmed one spring-fed place for seven thousand years.
sites.ex: Saudi Commission for Tourism and National Heritage; Al-Ahsa Municipality
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre. Al-Ahsa Oasis, an Evolving Cultural Landscape (ref. 1563), inscribed 2018.

sites.n: Rock Art of Jubbah and Shuwaymis
sites.s: Ten thousand years of carvings · World Heritage
sites.el: Petroglyphs above a vanished lake 20 km long
sites.te: Pictures beside a lake that dried
sites.se: Life-size humans, cattle and lions carved over 10,000 years on cliffs that once overlooked a lake
sites.sa: بشر وماشية وأسود بحجمها الطبيعي نُقشت على مدى 10,000 عام على جروف أطلّت يومًا على بحيرة
sites.desc: Two clusters of petroglyphs in Ha'il: Jabal Umm Sinman at Jubbah, above the bed of a Holocene lake about 20 by 5 km, and Jabal al-Manjor and Raat at Shuwaymis. The oldest carvings, of life-size people and wild animals, date back about 10,000 years; later panels show cattle herding, horses, camels and Thamudic inscriptions. Inscribed in 2015 under criteria (i) and (iii).
sites.sig: One of the largest and longest sequences of rock art in the world.
sites.ex: Saudi Commission for Tourism and National Heritage; Palaeodeserts Project (Max Planck Institute)

sites.s: Capital of Kinda · World Heritage
sites.el: Walled town, market, temples and 17 wells
sites.te: The city at the edge of the Empty Quarter
sites.se: A caravan capital with wall paintings, a market and temples, found under the sand at Wadi al-Dawasir
sites.sa: عاصمة قوافل بجدارياتها وسوقها ومعابدها، وُجدت تحت الرمل في وادي الدواسر
sites.desc: The capital of the kingdom of Kinda on the caravan route between Yemen and the Gulf, at a gap in the Tuwaiq escarpment facing the Rub' al Khali. Excavated by King Saud University from 1972, it has a walled market, houses with wall paintings, five temples, tombs and 17 wells, with South Arabian inscriptions and bronzes. Inscribed on 27 July 2024 as the Cultural Landscape of Al-Faw Archaeological Area.
sites.sig: The most complete pre-Islamic town in central Arabia and its first painted interiors.
sites.ex: King Saud University (A. R. al-Ansary) 1972 onwards; Heritage Commission and Saudi-French mission
disc: Wall paintings of a feasting man

sites.s: Rock art and ancient wells · World Heritage
sites.el: Bir Hima wells in use for 3,000 years
sites.te: Seven thousand years of travellers
sites.se: Rock art and inscriptions in many scripts beside wells that caravans still use
sites.sa: فنون صخرية ونقوش بخطوط عدة بجوار آبار ما زالت القوافل تستخدمها
sites.desc: A mountainous area north of Najran on one of Arabia's oldest caravan routes, with 34 rock-art sites carved over some 7,000 years: hunting, animals, plants and people, and inscriptions in Musnad, Thamudic, Greek and early Arabic. The Bir Hima wells have supplied travellers for about 3,000 years and still flow. Inscribed in 2021 under criterion (iii).
sites.sig: A roadside archive of every script that passed through southern Arabia.
sites.ex: Saudi Heritage Commission; Saudi-French Najran mission

sites.s: Dilmun-era island of Qatif
sites.el: Castle mound on 7,000 years of layers
sites.te: Seven thousand years under one castle
sites.ta: سبعة آلاف عام تحت قلعة واحدة
sites.se: An island off Qatif settled since about 5000 BC, with a Dilmun past and a Portuguese fort
sites.sa: جزيرة قبالة القطيف سُكنت منذ نحو 5000 ق.م، بماضٍ دلموني وحصن برتغالي
sites.desc: An island about 6 km off Qatif, joined to it by causeways, inhabited since about 5000 BC. Pottery of c. 4500 and 3000 BC was excavated by a Danish team in 1968, tombs date to c. 2000 BC and a 94 cm stone statue of a man, probably Sumerian in style, is in the National Museum in Riyadh. The island was a centre of the Dilmun world; Tarout Castle stands on the mound, with a Portuguese fort of 1515–1521 nearby.
sites.sig: The oldest continuously inhabited place on the Saudi Gulf coast.
sites.ex: Danish expedition (G. Bibby) 1968; Saudi Department of Antiquities

sites.s: Hellenistic walled city, possibly Gerrha
sites.el: Stone city wall and a gold funerary mask
sites.te: The girl with the golden mask
sites.se: A walled Hellenistic city 90 km inland from Jubail, where a child was buried with a mask of gold
sites.sa: مدينة هلنستية مسوّرة على بُعد 90 كم من الجبيل، دُفنت فيها طفلة بقناع من الذهب
sites.desc: A Hellenistic city about 90 km west of Jubail enclosed by a stone wall, settled from about 300 BC to AD 300 and possibly earlier; many scholars think it the site of Gerrha, the rich trading city Strabo described. A Danish mission (1968), a Saudi-British team (1983) and Saudi excavations from 2000 found houses, coins and, in a tomb, a young girl buried with a gold funerary mask, gloves and jewellery, now in the National Museum.
sites.sig: The richest burial of pre-Islamic eastern Arabia and the best candidate for lost Gerrha.
sites.ex: Danish expedition 1968; Saudi-UK 1983; Saudi Department of Antiquities 2000–2006; Saudi-French Thaj mission 2016 onwards

sites.s: Church of the East, 4th–7th century
sites.el: Nave, sanctuary and two carved crosses
sites.te: A church found at a picnic
sites.se: Picnickers found a buried church in 1986; its carved crosses still mark the doorway
sites.sa: عثر متنزهون على كنيسة مدفونة عام 1986؛ وما زالت صلبانها المنحوتة تعلّم المدخل
sites.desc: A church of the Church of the East near Jubail, found by picnickers in 1986 and excavated by the Saudi Department of Antiquities in 1987. Two crosses are carved either side of the doorway between nave and sanctuary. Its date is debated between the 4th and 7th centuries; it belongs to the chain of Christian communities along the Gulf known from Sir Bani Yas, Kharg and Failaka. The site is fenced and the excavation unpublished.
sites.sig: Evidence of the Christian communities of the Gulf coast before Islam.

sites.s: Lihyanite capital and open-air library
sites.te: A library carved in a canyon
sites.se: The capital of Dadan and Lihyan, and a canyon with 450 inscriptions in old Arabian scripts
sites.sa: عاصمة دادان ولحيان، ووادٍ فيه 450 نقشًا بالخطوط العربية القديمة
sites.desc: Dadan, in the AlUla valley, was the capital of the Dadanite and then Lihyanite kingdoms of the 1st millennium BC: a town below a cliff of tombs, some guarded by carved lions, and a sanctuary with statues of kings. Nearby Jabal Ikmah holds about 450 inscriptions in Dadanitic, an ancient North Arabian script, most from the second half of the 1st millennium BC, recording rituals, taxes and names. Jabal Ikmah joined UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in May 2023.
sites.sig: The largest concentration of Dadanitic texts, a step on the road to Arabic.
sites.ex: King Saud University 2004 onwards; Royal Commission for AlUla with French CNRS mission

sites.s: Coral-stone port · World Heritage
sites.el: Tower houses of coral stone with wooden rawashin
sites.te: A city built from the reef
sites.se: The port of Makkah since the 7th century, its tall houses built of coral stone and screened in wood
sites.sa: ميناء مكة منذ القرن السابع، بيوته العالية من حجر المرجان ومزيّنة بالرواشين
sites.desc: The old walled town of Jeddah, made the port of Makkah by Caliph Uthman in the 7th century, grew rich on pilgrim and Indian Ocean trade. Its tower houses are built of coral stone quarried from the Red Sea reef and faced with large wooden rawashin, with mosques, ribats and suqs between them. About a third of the original walled city is inscribed (2014, criteria ii, iv, vi); the Ministry of Culture began a large restoration in 2021.
sites.sig: The last Red Sea merchant town still standing in coral stone.
sites.ex: Ministry of Culture, Jeddah Historic District Program
disc: Port of Makkah since the 7th century
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre. Historic Jeddah, the Gate to Makkah (ref. 1361), inscribed 2014.

sites.s: Herders’ shelter in a lava tube
sites.te: People who lived in a lava tube
sites.se: The first excavated lava tube in Arabia sheltered herders for thousands of years
sites.sa: أول أنبوب بركاني يُنقَّب في الجزيرة العربية آوى الرعاة آلاف السنين
sites.desc: A lava tube about 1.5 km long in the Harrat Khaybar lava field, the first in Arabia to be excavated. Stone tools, animal bones and charcoal show repeated use from about 10,000 to 7,000 years ago and into the Bronze Age by groups herding cattle, sheep and goats; rock art at the entrance shows herding and dogs, and human remains record diets that gained fruit and cereals when oasis farming arrived. Published in PLOS ONE in 2024.
sites.sig: The first proof that people used Arabia's lava caves as shelters on the move.
sites.ex: Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology, Heritage Commission and Saudi Geological Survey (Stewart et al.)
disc: Rock art of herders with dogs
refs: Stewart, M., Andrieux, E., Blinkhorn, J. et al. (2024). First evidence for human occupation of a lava tube in Arabia. PLOS ONE 19(4).

sites.s: Tuwaiq escarpment of Jurassic limestone
sites.el: Cliffs about 300 m above an ancient sea bed
sites.te: A reef 800 km long
sites.se: The Tuwaiq escarpment is Jurassic sea floor, lifted and cut into cliffs that run 800 km
sites.sa: جرف طويق قاع بحر جوراسي، رُفع وقُطع إلى جروف تمتد 800 كم
sites.desc: The Tuwaiq escarpment runs some 800 km through Najd from Qassim to Wadi al-Dawasir, a wall of Middle Jurassic Tuwaiq Mountain limestone up to 600 m high laid down in a shallow sea with coral bioherms. At Jebel Fihrayn, about 100 km north-west of Riyadh, the cliff stands 1,131 m above sea level and drops about 300 m to the plain, with the view that earned it the name Edge of the World. The same limestone holds Callovian corals and, at depth, the reservoirs of the Arab Formation.
sites.sig: The spine of central Arabia and the outcrop of the rocks that hold its oil.
sites.ex: Saudi Geological Survey; King Saud University geology

sites.s: Lava field that reached Madinah
sites.el: Lava flow 23 km long, 4 km short of the city
sites.te: The night the lava came to Madinah
sites.se: In 1256 a fissure opened and lava flowed 23 km, stopping 4 km from Madinah
sites.sa: في 1256 انشقّ الأرض وسالت الحمم 23 كم، وتوقفت على بُعد 4 كم من المدينة
sites.desc: The largest lava field in Saudi Arabia, stretching about 300 km south of Madinah and rising to 1,744 m. In 1256 AD (654 AH) an eruption on its northern edge lasted 52 days, poured out about 0.5 km³ of basalt in a flow 23 km long that stopped 4 km from Madinah, and was recorded by the city's chroniclers; an earlier eruption is dated to AD 641. Earthquake swarms in 1999 and 2009 (at Harrat Lunayyir) show the fields are not extinct.
sites.sig: The best-documented historic eruption in Arabia, written down by eyewitnesses.
disc: Flow stopped 4 km from the city

sites.s: Maar crater of Harrat Kishb
sites.el: 2.2 km wide, 250 m deep, salt floor
sites.te: A bowl blown out by steam
sites.se: Rising magma met groundwater and blew a crater 2 km across; salt now floors it
sites.sa: التقت الصهارة الصاعدة بالمياه الجوفية فنسفت فوهة بعرض 2 كم؛ يغطي قاعها الملح اليوم
sites.desc: A maar about 2.2 km across and 250 m deep in the Harrat Kishb lava field between Taif and Madinah, formed when basaltic magma met groundwater and exploded through steam. Its floor is a white pan of sodium phosphate and salt crystals; its walls expose the layered tuff and the older lavas. Dated to about 1.15 million years. Once thought a meteorite crater, it is now a popular hike with a trail to the floor.
sites.sig: The largest and clearest maar crater in Arabia.
sites.ex: Saudi Geological Survey; King Abdulaziz University
refs: Abdel Wahab, A., Abul-Maaty, M., Stuart, F. M. et al. (2014). Volcanic history of Al Wahbah maar, Saudi Arabia. Journal of African Earth Sciences 92, 1–13.

sites.s: Iron meteorite impact in the Rub’ al Khali
sites.te: The place of iron
sites.se: An iron meteorite of more than 3,500 tonnes struck the dunes and left glass and craters that Philby found in 1932
sites.sa: نيزك حديدي يزيد على 3,500 طن ضرب الكثبان وخلّف زجاجًا وفوهات وجدها فيلبي عام 1932
sites.desc: A group of impact craters, the largest about 116 m across, in the sands of the Rub' al Khali, reached by H. St John Philby on 2 February 1932 while searching for the lost city of Ubar; the Bedouin called it Al Hadida, the place of iron. An iron meteorite estimated at more than 3,500 tonnes exploded on impact, leaving black glass pellets, bleached impactite with coesite and iron fragments including the 2.2-tonne Camel's Hump now in Riyadh. Thermoluminescence dating puts the fall within the last 250 years or so; the dunes are burying the craters.
sites.sig: One of the few impact sites on Earth preserved in sand, and among the youngest.
sites.ex: Philby 1932; Zahid–USGS expeditions (J. C. Wynn, E. M. Shoemaker) 1994–95
refs: Wynn, J. C. & Shoemaker, E. M. (1998). The day the sands caught fire. Scientific American 279(5), 64–71.

sites.s: Where Saudi oil was found, 1938
sites.te: The well that would not give up
sites.se: After six dry wells, No. 7 found oil at 1,440 m in the Arab Formation and flowed for 44 years
sites.sa: بعد ست آبار جافة، وجدت البئر رقم 7 النفط على عمق 1,440 م في تكوين العرب وتدفقت 44 عامًا
sites.desc: On the Dammam Dome, the first six wells drilled by CASOC from 1935 found little. On 3 March 1938 well No. 7, deepened on the advice of geologist Max Steineke, struck oil at 1,440 m in the Jurassic Arab Formation and flowed at over 1,500 barrels a day. It produced about 32 million barrels until it was shut in 1982, and is preserved as a monument in Dhahran. The dome is a salt-cored anticline, the same structure that holds Bahrain's and Qatar's fields.
sites.sig: The well that started the Saudi oil industry.
disc: Oil at 1,440 m in the Arab Formation
refs: Saudi Aramco. Dammam No. 7: the Prosperity Well.

sites.s: Dunes 300 m high over an oil field
sites.el: Linear dunes up to 333 m, sabkha floors
sites.te: Sand a hundred storeys high
sites.se: Red dunes 300 m tall in the Empty Quarter, with an oil field found in 1968 beneath them
sites.sa: كثبان حمراء بارتفاع 300 م في الربع الخالي، تحتها حقل نفط اكتُشف عام 1968
sites.desc: In the north-east of the Rub' al Khali, about 800 km south of Dhahran, long red dunes rise up to 333 m above floors of sabkha; they belong to the largest continuous sand sea on Earth. Oil was found beneath them by the Shaybah-1 well in 1968, and the field, with about 14 billion barrels of proved reserves, was developed in 1995–98 and reached 1 million barrels a day in 2016. A 637 km² wildlife sanctuary around the plant holds more than 40 Arabian oryx and 70 sand gazelles.
sites.sig: The tallest dunes of Arabia, and a working oil field in the emptiest place on Earth.
sites.ex: Saudi Aramco; Saudi Geological Survey (Rub’ al Khali sands)
refs: Saudipedia. Shaybah Oil Field.

sites.s: Oryx reserve on the Empty Quarter · World Heritage
sites.te: Where the oryx came home
sites.se: The Arabian oryx, extinct in the wild in 1972, was released here in 1995 and now breeds free
sites.sa: المها العربي، الذي انقرض في البرية عام 1972، أُطلق هنا عام 1995 ويتكاثر حرًا اليوم
sites.desc: A reserve of 12,750 km² on the western edge of the Rub' al Khali, where the Tuwaiq escarpment meets the sand sea. Protected in 1994, it received the first Arabian oryx released back into the wild in 1995 after the species had been lost from the wild in 1972; it also holds sand gazelle, mountain gazelle, Nubian ibex and about 120 plant species. Inscribed in September 2023 as Saudi Arabia's first natural World Heritage site under criteria (vii) and (ix).
sites.sig: The largest oryx reintroduction in the world and the first natural World Heritage site of the kingdom.
sites.ex: National Center for Wildlife; formerly NCWCD

sites.s: Red Sea archipelago · Biosphere Reserve
sites.te: Gazelles on a coral island
sites.se: Eighty-four islands of raised reef, home to Saudi Arabia’s largest gazelle herd, mangroves and nesting seabirds
sites.sa: أربع وثمانون جزيرة من شعاب مرفوعة، موطن أكبر قطيع غزلان في السعودية، والقرم والطيور البحرية
sites.desc: An archipelago of more than 84 islands about 42 km off Jazan, built of uplifted coral limestone that stands 10–20 m and locally 75 m above the sea. Protected in 1989 and Saudi Arabia's first UNESCO Biosphere Reserve in September 2021, the 5,408 km² reserve is 90 percent marine: coral reefs, seagrass, three of the Red Sea's thirteen red-mangrove stands, dugong, green and hawksbill turtles, and nesting pink-backed pelicans, sooty falcons and crab-plovers. The islands carry the largest population of the Farasan (idmi) gazelle.
sites.sig: The richest island ecosystem of the Saudi Red Sea.
sites.ex: National Center for Wildlife; Khaled bin Sultan Living Oceans Foundation surveys 2006
disc: Largest gazelle population in the kingdom

sites.s: Seagrass, dugong and flamingos on the Gulf
sites.el: About 2,410 km² of bays and islands
sites.te: A coast that healed
sites.se: Hit by the 1991 oil spill, the bays north of Jubail were protected and now hold dugong, turtles and a flamingo colony
sites.sa: بعد تسرب النفط عام 1991، حُميت الخلجان شمال الجبيل وتضم اليوم الأتوم والسلاحف ومستعمرة فلامنغو
sites.desc: A protected area of about 2,410 km² of shallow bays, islands and sabkha between Jubail and the Kuwaiti border, the coast most heavily oiled by the 1991 Gulf War spill. Set up by the NCWCD in the early 1990s, it protects seagrass meadows, coral patches, mangroves and mudflats used by several hundred dugong, green and hawksbill turtles, dolphins and a breeding colony of greater flamingos; the Sabkhat al-Fasl lagoons nearby are a Key Biodiversity Area for waterbirds.
sites.sig: The main recovery site for the Gulf coast after the largest oil spill in history.
sites.ex: National Center for Wildlife; Royal Commission for Jubail; EU-Gulf War damage assessment 1992

sites.n: Raydah Reserve and the Asir Junipers
sites.s: Cloud forest of Arabia
sites.te: A forest in the clouds
sites.se: Juniper woods between 2,500 and 3,000 m hold the Asir magpie, found nowhere else on Earth
sites.sa: غابات العرعر بين 2,500 و3,000 م تضم عقعق عسير الذي لا يوجد في أي مكان آخر على الأرض
sites.desc: About 1,200 ha of the Asir escarpment west of Abha, falling from about 2,800 m to Wadi Jaw at 1,350 m, protected since 1989 for the densest juniper woodland in the kingdom. The junipers grow between 2,500 and 3,000 m where monsoon cloud brings moisture, and shelter most of Arabia's endemic birds, including the Asir magpie, estimated at only about 135 pairs. Drought, grazing and development threaten the trees; Soudah Development has planted some 165,000 native trees in the highlands.

sites.s: Red Sea reef lagoon of 92 islands
sites.te: Ninety-two islands, nine untouched
sites.ta: اثنتان وتسعون جزيرة، تسع منها بلا مساس
sites.se: A reef lagoon planned so that 58 percent is conserved and development covers 5 percent
sites.sa: بحيرة شعابية خُطط لها بحيث يُحفظ 58% منها ولا يتجاوز العمران 5%
sites.desc: A lagoon of 2,081 km² enclosed by a barrier reef on the northern Red Sea coast, with 92 islands, coral reefs, seagrass beds and mangroves and species of global conservation concern. In 2020 KAUST scientists led by Carlos Duarte published a marine spatial plan for the Red Sea Project here that conserves 58 percent of the marine area and limits development to about 5 percent, aiming for a 30 percent net conservation gain. The reef corals of the northern Red Sea are among the most heat-tolerant known.
sites.sig: A test of whether tourism can be built around a reef without losing it.

sites.s: Walled oasis city of Nabonidus · Saudi-German excavations
sites.te: The king who left Babylon
sites.se: An oasis ringed by 15 km of wall, where the last king of Babylon lived for ten years
sites.sa: واحة يحيط بها سور طوله 15 كم، عاش فيها آخر ملوك بابل عشر سنوات
sites.desc: An oasis city between the Hijaz mountains and the Nafud, with a main mound of more than 200 acres and a sandstone-and-mud-brick wall of just over 15 km enclosing oasis, fields and part of a dried lake; parts of the wall date to 2500–2000 BC and it stood by the end of the second millennium BC. Carnelian bead-making and flint working go back to about 4000 BC, a temple was in use from the 12th to 9th centuries BC, and a 2010 find carried the name of pharaoh Ramesses III, the first pharaonic inscription found in Saudi Arabia. The Babylonian king Nabonidus moved here in 556 BC and stayed about a decade; a sandstone stela showing him was found near the main temple. Saudi-German excavations under the German Archaeological Institute began in 2004.
sites.sig: The only place outside Mesopotamia where a Babylonian king ruled for a decade, and one of the longest-lived oases in Arabia.

sites.s: Nabataean-founded hill fort · Al-Jawf
sites.el: Four conical towers about 12 m tall
sites.te: The fortress that rebelled
sites.se: A hill fort on Nabataean foundations that Queen Zenobia of Palmyra could not take
sites.sa: حصن على تلة بأسس نبطية عجزت الملكة زنوبيا التدمرية عن اقتحامه
sites.desc: A fortress on a hill about 620 m above sea level overlooking the oasis of Dumat al-Jandal, 50 km from Sakaka. Excavations in 1976 and by Khaleel al-Moaqil in 1986 found Nabataean and Roman pottery of the 1st–2nd centuries AD, placing its foundations in the Nabataean period. The medieval geographer Yaqut recorded the siege by Zenobia of Palmyra in the 3rd century AD, who could not take it. It has two storeys, stone below and mud brick above, four conical towers about 12 m high and two wells; it was damaged by cannon in 1853, besieged for ten months in 1909, and restored in 1995–2003 and again from 2018.
sites.sig: One of the few forts in Arabia with a documented history running from the Nabataeans to the 20th century.

sites.s: Chalcolithic standing stones · Sakaka
sites.el: 54 groups of pillars up to 3 m tall
sites.te: The stone men of Al-Jawf
sites.se: Fifty-four clusters of sandstone pillars raised 6,000 years ago, called "the men" because they look like a crowd from afar
sites.sa: أربع وخمسون مجموعة من أعمدة الحجر الرملي أُقيمت قبل 6,000 عام، سُمّيت «الرجال» لأنها تبدو كحشد من بعيد
sites.desc: Fifty-four groups of trimmed sandstone pillars, each group of 2 to 19 stones and the tallest about 3 m, in the Qara suburb south-east of Sakaka. Excavated by the Saudi General Administration of Antiquities and Museums in 1975–1976, which found scrapers, awls, blades and pottery confirming a Copper Age date of about 6,000 years ago; later finds include obsidian, sandstone vessels and beads, and two wells of the fifth millennium BC drawing water from 4–5 m down. Some pillars carry later Thamudic inscriptions. Aerial imagery suggests a rough alignment to sunrise and sunset, and the current view is a complex of small sanctuaries on the Wadi Sirhan corridor.
sites.sig: Among the oldest standing-stone monuments in Arabia, older than Stonehenge.

sites.s: Walled caravan city of Najran · excavated since 1979
sites.p: Pre-Islamic South Arabian to early Islamic
sites.te: The city of the ditch
sites.se: A fortified town on the incense road, remembered for the massacre of its Christians in the 520s
sites.sa: بلدة محصّنة على طريق البخور، تُذكر بمذبحة مسيحييها في عشرينيات القرن السادس
sites.desc: The oldest part of Najran, south-east of the modern city near Bir Hima, occupied from at least 500 BC; its largest structure is a fort of stone and mud brick of the 1st century BC. A stop on the frankincense and myrrh route, briefly held by the Roman prefect Gallus around 25 BC. In the 520s the Himyarite king Dhu Nuwas massacred the town's Christians, events alluded to in the Quranic chapter al-Buruj, from which the name 'the ditch' comes; residents moved to present-day Najran in the 620s. Excavated by the Saudi Ministry of Culture since 1979 and with CNRS from 2016; finds announced in 2023 include three gold rings, a bronze bull's head, Attic pottery of the 3rd century BC and a granite inscription 48 cm high and 2.3 m long.
sites.sig: A place where South Arabian paganism, Christianity, Judaism and Islam all left traces within one walled town.

sites.s: Bronze Age walled oasis town · found 2024
sites.te: A town hidden in the lava
sites.se: A 4,000-year-old town of 500 people inside a rampart-ringed oasis, found in 2024
sites.sa: بلدة عمرها 4,000 عام سكنها 500 شخص داخل واحة محاطة بسور، اكتُشفت عام 2024
sites.desc: A Bronze Age town of about 2.6 hectares in the Khaybar oasis, built around 2400–2000 BC and occupied until about 1500–1300 BC, with residential and funerary areas inside the fortifications and burials in stepped tower tombs. About 500 people lived there, grinding food, making and trading pottery, working metal, growing cereals and keeping animals. The find, published in PLOS ONE in 2024 by Guillaume Charloux's Khaybar Longue Durée project (CNRS with the Royal Commission for AlUla and AFALULA), suggests settled town life began in the oasis in the second half of the third millennium BC, when the region was thought to be purely pastoral.
sites.sig: The first Bronze Age town found in north-west Arabia, pushing back the start of urban life there by a thousand years.

sites.s: Abbasid pilgrim station on Darb Zubaydah · King Saud University excavations
sites.el: Palace of 13 rooms around a courtyard
sites.te: A station on the road to Mecca
sites.se: A pasture reserve of the early caliphs that grew into an Abbasid town on the Kufa–Mecca pilgrim road
sites.sa: حِمى من عهد الخلفاء الراشدين نما ليصبح بلدة عباسية على درب الحج بين الكوفة ومكة
sites.desc: A settlement about 200 km north-east of Medina that began as a pasture reserve (hima) under the first caliphs, grew into a town in the Umayyad period and peaked in the early Abbasid era of the 3rd century AH (9th century AD) as a major station on Darb Zubaydah, the pilgrim road from Kufa to Mecca. The companion Abu Dharr al-Ghifari spent his last years and died here. Excavations by King Saud University revealed fortified residential quarters, palaces, two mosques, an industrial area with a glass furnace, a circular reservoir and many domestic water tanks; the main palace has 13 rooms opening onto a central courtyard, and houses were of sun-dried mud brick on stone foundations. Finds include pottery, coins, inscriptions and jewellery.
sites.sig: One of the best-excavated early Islamic towns in Arabia and a key to the archaeology of the pilgrim roads.

sites.s: Stone village on a white marble hill · Al-Baha
sites.el: 49 stone houses of up to four storeys
sites.te: A village on a white hill
sites.se: Forty-nine stone houses stacked on a marble outcrop above a spring-fed valley
sites.sa: تسع وأربعون بيتاً حجرياً تتراصّ فوق نتوء رخامي يعلو وادياً تغذيه عين ماء
sites.desc: A village in the Al-Mikhwah district of Al-Baha, about 20 km south-west of Al-Makhwah, established in the 10th century AH (16th century AD) and named after the water that flows from the mountains beside it. It has 49 houses, 9 of one storey, 19 of two, 11 of three and 10 of four, with a mosque by the stream; a historical source reports high-quality marble in the area. The Saudi Tourism Authority allocated 16 million riyals to a three-phase, five-year rehabilitation that reopened the mosque and turned buildings into a museum and visitor centre. It is on UNESCO's tentative list as 'Zee Ain Heritage Village in Al-Baha Region'.
sites.sig: The most striking example of the stone-tower villages of the Sarawat, set on a hill of white rock.

sites.s: Stone-tower village of Asir · UNESCO tentative list
sites.el: About 60 palaces of up to eight floors
sites.te: Towers of stone and colour
sites.se: Sixty stone, clay and wood palaces, their rooms painted in Al-Qatt patterns, on the old road from Yemen
sites.sa: ستون قصراً من الحجر والطين والخشب، زُيّنت غرفها بنقوش القطّ، على الطريق القديم من اليمن
sites.desc: A village about 45–50 km west of Abha with around 60 multi-storey buildings of natural stone, clay and wood, some reaching eight floors, with coloured wooden windows and interior walls painted in the Al-Qatt style. Mentioned as a civic centre in 550 AH (1155 AD) and as capital of the Hilli emirate in 730 AH (1329 AD), it linked Yemen and the Levant through Mecca and Medina. Al Al-wan Palace, more than four centuries old, houses a heritage museum opened in 1987 with over 2,000 objects. Rehabilitated from 2015 with the private sector, awarded the Prince Sultan bin Salman Prize for Urban Heritage in 2017, and submitted to UNESCO's tentative list on 8 April 2015 under criteria (iv) and (v).
sites.sig: The finest surviving ensemble of Asir's stone-tower architecture and painted interiors.

sites.s: Oldest stone-tool site in Saudi Arabia · Al-Jawf
sites.te: The first toolmakers of Arabia
sites.se: Choppers and spheroids of quartzite left by early humans over a million years ago
sites.sa: فؤوس وأحجار كروية من الكوارتزيت تركها إنسان قديم قبل أكثر من مليون عام
sites.desc: A broad canyon about 45 km north-west of Sakaka where a joint American-Saudi team recorded, in 1985, a horseshoe-shaped site almost 5 km long with 16 artefact concentrations spaced 200–350 m apart. It yielded 1,517 quartzite choppers, polyhedrons, spheroids and discoids of the Developed Oldowan tradition first defined at Olduvai Gorge, dated to more than one million years ago, the oldest found in Saudi Arabia. The site had been discovered in 1977 under the Comprehensive Archaeological Survey Program; Saudipedia records 17 settlements and 1,884 tools in all, some linked to about 1.3 million years ago, and later rock art of camels and ibex on a nearby hill.
sites.sig: The earliest evidence of human presence in Saudi Arabia.

sites.s: Jabal Abyad, Jabal Bayda and Jabal Qidr · active lava field
sites.dr: Last 5 million years; last eruption 7th century AD
sites.te: Black and white volcanoes
sites.se: A pale rhyolite dome and tuff cone beside a black stratovolcano, in a 14,000 km² lava field
sites.sa: قبة ريوليتية شاحبة ومخروط رمادي إلى جوار بركان أسود، في حقل حمم مساحته 14,000 كم²
sites.desc: Harrat Khaybar covers about 14,000 km² of western Saudi Arabia, built by eruptions over the past 5 million years along a 100 km north-south vent system; eight lava flows are younger than 1,500 years and the last reported eruption was in the 7th century. At its heart stand three young vents: Jabal Qidr, a basaltic stratovolcano with a 400 m summit crater and the only stratovolcano in the western harrats; Jabal Abyad, a dome of thick silica-rich rhyolitic lava rising above 2,090 m, the highest point of the harrats; and Jabal Bayda, a tuff cone with a crater about 1,400 m wide formed when magma met groundwater. The white colour comes from ash of comenditic lavas; 'abyad' and 'bayda' both mean white.
sites.sig: The clearest place in Arabia to see black basalt and white silica-rich volcanoes side by side.
sites.ex: NASA Earth Observatory (Landsat 9, 2024); Saudi Geological Survey

sites.s: Earthquake swarm and surface rupture · Nature Geoscience 2010
sites.p: Red Sea rifting, Neogene to present
sites.dr: Lava field of the last 30 million years; crisis April – June 2009
sites.te: The ground that split in 2009
sites.se: More than 30,000 earthquakes and a 10 km dyke that nearly reached the surface forced 30,000 people from their homes
sites.sa: أكثر من 30,000 زلزال وقاطع صخري بطول 10 كم كاد يبلغ السطح أجبر 30,000 شخص على مغادرة منازلهم
sites.desc: A lava field in north-west Saudi Arabia, one of the harrats formed along the Red Sea over the past 30 million years. From April to June 2009 a swarm of more than 30,000 earthquakes, six of them magnitude 4.6 to 5.7 at the peak of 17–20 May, accompanied the intrusion of a near-vertical north-west-trending dyke about 10 km long that almost reached the surface. Radar interferometry showed over 1 m of east-west extension across a 40 km × 40 km area and more than 40 cm of uplift, with an 8 km surface rupture of 91 cm offset. Saudi civil protection evacuated more than 30,000 people. The Nature Geoscience study concluded that rift margins stay active sites of extension, not only the central Red Sea axis.
sites.sig: The best-recorded magma intrusion in Arabia, proving the Red Sea margin is still pulling apart.
sites.ex: Saudi Geological Survey; US Geological Survey (J. Pallister et al.); KAUST (S. Jónsson)

sites.s: Joint-controlled canyons in the Hofuf Formation · Al-Ahsa
sites.el: Boxwork of linear passages, cool all year
sites.te: A mountain of cool corridors
sites.se: Deep fissures in soft sandstone and marl widened into tall passages that stay cool in summer
sites.sa: شقوق عميقة في حجر رملي ومارل لين اتسعت إلى ممرات عالية تبقى باردة في الصيف
sites.desc: An outlier mesa about 13 km east of Hofuf at the eastern edge of the Shedgum Plateau, cut into calcareous sandstone, marl and clay of the Upper Miocene to Lower Pliocene Hofuf Formation. A 2006 study in the Journal of Cave and Karst Studies found that its tall, linear passages and narrow canyons formed by erosional enlargement of very deep, narrow joint-controlled fissures, the best-developed boxwork of its kind in the Eastern Province. The caves stay much cooler than the air outside with an almost constant temperature, and were used to store grain and shelter travellers. The mountain is part of the Al-Ahsa Oasis cultural landscape inscribed by UNESCO in 2018.
sites.sig: A rare example of caves made by joints and weathering rather than by dissolving limestone.

sites.s: Anhydrite sinkhole with an underground lake · Al-Kharj
sites.dr: Surveyed 1938; lake 120 m below the surface
sites.el: Entrance 74 m wide, cave 180–200 m deep
sites.te: A lake under the desert
sites.se: A collapse cave where the first anhydrite in the kingdom was identified and a cold lake lies 120 m down
sites.sa: كهف انهياري تعرّف فيه الجيولوجيون على أول أنهيدريت في المملكة، وتقبع فيه بحيرة باردة على عمق 120 م
sites.desc: A solutional cave about 30–40 km south-east of Riyadh near Al-Kharj, in a hill of limestone and anhydrite. Its entrance is about 74 m wide and the cave descends 180–200 m on a widening slope to an underground lake about 120 m below the surface, an opening into a vast groundwater reservoir whose water was once drawn by caravans. Geologists came at the invitation of King Abdulaziz for the first surface exploration of anhydrite rock in Saudi Arabia, in 1938 according to Wikipedia; Swedish divers later tracked its water-filled passages. It is one of 1,826 caves recorded across the kingdom and is listed by the Quality of Life programme among the top fourteen landmarks of Riyadh Province, though rockfalls make the descent dangerous.
sites.sig: The most accessible window into the great aquifer beneath central Arabia.
sites.ex: Saudi Geological Survey; Quality of Life Program (Vision 2030)

sites.s: Largest conventional oil field on Earth · discovered 1948
sites.dr: Reservoir c. 150 million years old; produced since 1951
sites.te: The king of giant fields
sites.se: An anticline 280 km long whose Jurassic carbonates have yielded more than 60 billion barrels
sites.sa: طيّة محدّبة بطول 280 كم أنتجت كربوناتها الجوراسية أكثر من 60 مليار برميل
sites.desc: Discovered in 1948 with the Ain Dar test well about 200 km east of Riyadh, the first post-war find in the country, followed by Haradh (1949), Uthmaniyah (1951), Shedgum (1952) and Hawiyah (1953). The field follows the En Nala anticline, trending N15°E on a basement horst, about 280 km long and 30 km wide with a productive area of about 2,800 km². The main reservoir is the Upper Jurassic Arab-D carbonate, with an oil column of 396 m, average porosity about 15% and oil of 30–34° API, sealed by 30–100 m of anhydrite and sourced from the Hanifa and Tuwaiq formations. Production began in 1951 at 126,000 barrels a day, peaked at 5.7 million in 1981, and cumulative output reached 66 billion barrels by 2007.
sites.sig: No other single structure has supplied so much of the world's oil.

sites.s: Granite peak of the Midian mountains · snow most winters
sites.dr: Rock art said to be c. 10,000 BC; snow every winter
sites.te: The almond mountain of snow
sites.se: A light granite peak above the Gulf of Aqaba, highest in Midian, dusted with snow almost every winter
sites.sa: قمة من الغرانيت الفاتح تعلو خليج العقبة، الأعلى في جبال مدين، يكسوها الثلج كل شتاء تقريباً
sites.desc: The highest peak of the Midian mountains in Tabuk Province, about 200 km north-west of Tabuk and north-east of Al-Bad', rising to 2,549 m (Saudipedia) or 2,556–2,580 m (Wikipedia) with a prominence of about 1,600 m. The peak is a light-coloured calc-alkaline granite cut by east-trending rhyolite and andesite dykes, mapped by Brown, Johnson and Trent for the Directorate General of Mineral Resources in 1967, and is surrounded mostly by sandy terrain; valleys drain to Wadi Afal, Wadi Reem and Wadi al-Abyad. It receives snow almost every winter, has rock drawings, ancient inscriptions and Islamic writings, and is named after its almond trees. The range lies within the NEOM area.
sites.sig: One of the few places in Arabia where snow falls regularly, on some of the peninsula's oldest rock.

sites.s: Wind-carved sandstone monolith · AlUla
sites.dr: Rock 540 – 485 million years old; uplifted 30 million years ago
sites.te: An elephant made of sand
sites.se: A 52 m sandstone outcrop sculpted by rain, wind and sand into the shape of an elephant
sites.sa: نتوء من الحجر الرملي بارتفاع 52 م نحتته الأمطار والرياح والرمال على هيئة فيل
sites.desc: A sandstone monolith 52 m high at AlUla in north-west Saudi Arabia, eroded by rain, wind and blown sand over millions of years into the form of an elephant with its trunk touching the ground. The AlUla sandstones were laid down about 540–485 million years ago and uplifted about 30 million years ago when the Red Sea began to open, according to the Royal Commission for AlUla's geology notes. It is the best-known of the sandstone outcrops of the AlUla valley and a centre of night-sky tourism since the region's dark-sky park opened in 2024.
sites.sig: The most photographed rock in Saudi Arabia and a textbook example of differential erosion.

sites.s: Sandstone canyon with year-round springs · Tabuk
sites.dr: Canyon of about 18 km; tentative list since 2023
sites.te: The valley of palms
sites.se: Red sandstone columns and cliffs up to 500 m frame a stream that flows all year through palms and oleander
sites.sa: أعمدة وجروف من الحجر الرملي الأحمر يصل ارتفاعها إلى 500 م تحيط بجدول يجري طوال العام بين النخيل والدفلى
sites.desc: A valley in south-west Tabuk Province, about 220 km from Tabuk, running about 125 km from north-east to south-west towards the Red Sea, with a linear canyon section of about 18 km through red sandstone columns and cliffs up to 500 m high shaped by water and wind. Freshwater springs flow all year, supporting palms, citrus, jujube, mint, papyrus, oleander and sedge. The canyon holds Nabataean rock-cut tomb facades and early Arabic inscriptions, and lies north-west of the Prince Mohammed bin Salman Nature Reserve. A 2025 Geoheritage study rated it a geomorphosite of high scientific value, and it has been on UNESCO's tentative list since 2023 as part of the 'Bioclimatic Refugia of Western Arabia'.
sites.sig: A living canyon where water, rock and Nabataean history meet in one of the driest regions on Earth.

sites.s: Hottest spring of the Red Sea coast · geothermal field
sites.dr: Rift heat of the last 30 million years; studied 2024
sites.te: Rain that comes back boiling
sites.se: Rainwater that sinks along rift fractures and returns at up to 81 °C from a reservoir of 150–205 °C
sites.sa: مياه أمطار تغور عبر صدوع الأخدود وتعود بحرارة تصل إلى 81 درجة من خزان حرارته 150–205 درجات
sites.desc: The hottest of four hot springs in the Al-Lith area of western Saudi Arabia, discharging water at 56–81 °C. A 2024 study in ACS Omega found the water to be of meteoric origin (rainwater), moderately alkaline sodium-bicarbonate type with 1,830–2,055 mg/L dissolved solids, and estimated a reservoir temperature of 150–205 °C from Na-K-Ca, K/Mg and quartz geothermometers, a medium-to-high-enthalpy system linked to Red Sea rifting. Magnetotelluric soundings published in 2024 imaged a fracture zone carrying fluids to the surface and a conductive body below 3.5 km interpreted as the heat source. The spring is also a local bathing destination.
sites.sig: Saudi Arabia's best-studied geothermal prospect, where the Red Sea rift heats the ground within reach of a drill.

sites.desc: A reserve of 2,244 km² on the arid plains 170 km north-east of Taif, protected since 1988 and fully enclosed by about 220 km of 2.1 m chain-link fence completed by March 1989. It was set aside mainly as a reintroduction site for the Arabian oryx, Arabian sand (reem) gazelle, Macqueen's bustard (houbara) and the North African red-necked ostrich, released from captive breeding. Wikipedia gives the area as 220,000 ha. It is listed by BirdLife as an Important Bird Area and managed by the National Center for Wildlife (formerly the Saudi Wildlife Authority).

sites.s: Nubian ibex canyons of the Tuwaiq escarpment · since 1988
sites.te: Lords of the sandstone canyons
sites.se: A rugged plateau of the Tuwaiq range where ibex recovered from a few dozen to more than 300

sites.desc: A reserve of 1,840.9 km² about 180 km south of Riyadh, between Al-Hariq and Hawtat Bani Tamim, covering a rugged plateau of the Tuwaiq mountain range cut by wadis and ravines, with western edges reaching 1,097 m. Declared a special ibex reserve in 1988 by the National Commission for Wildlife Conservation and Development after local villagers had informally kept grazing out of the central canyons; a 1995 Aramco World account by Khushal Habibi reported ibex rising from a few dozen to more than 300 after the hunting ban. Arabian gazelles were relocated here in 1990 and thrived. Acacia, Ziziphus and Haloxylon grow in the valleys.

sites.te: Islands of the doves
sites.se: Two coral islets off Al-Qunfudhah where doves, egrets, pelicans and ospreys breed over living reefs
sites.sa: جزيرتان مرجانيتان قبالة القنفذة يتكاثر فيها القماري والبلشون والبجع والعقاب النسّاري فوق شعاب حيّة
sites.desc: Two small islands, Umm al-Qamari al-Braniah and al-Fuqaniah, south-west of Al-Qunfudhah on the Red Sea coast, with a reported area of 4.03 km² in the World Database on Protected Areas. Listed as a protected area in 1977, they are described as the first protected area in Saudi Arabia (Saudipedia gives 1988 for the reserve's formal establishment). They are named after the turtle doves that gather on them in migration, and host collared doves, herons and egrets, pelicans, gulls and osprey; the reefs around the outer island are diverse and mostly living, and the vegetation includes Salvadora persica and Suaeda. Managed by the National Center for Wildlife.

sites.s: Basalt plateau of wolves, hyenas and houbara · since 1987
sites.te: Life on the black stones
sites.se: A huge lava plateau in the far north where 22 mammal species, including wolf, hyena and caracal, were recorded
sites.sa: هضبة بركانية شاسعة في أقصى الشمال سُجّل فيها 22 نوعاً من الثدييات، منها الذئب والضبع والوشق
sites.desc: A volcanic plateau of black basalt in the far north of Saudi Arabia, with low volcanic hills between 800 and 1,150 m, covering about 13,775 km² (12,150 km² in the 1997 survey); one of the first reserves created by the Saudi wildlife authority, in 1987 (1986 in the survey). Surveys from 1991 to 1996 by Seddon, Van Heezik and Nader confirmed 22 mammal species including eight native carnivores, among them the Arabian wolf, striped hyena and caracal, as well as goitered gazelle, red fox, hare and jerboa. Birds include houbara bustard, golden eagle and nine species of lark, and the wadis carry Lycium, Tamarix and Calligonum.
sites.sig: The largest of the kingdom's early reserves and its best stronghold for large desert carnivores.

sites.s: Former royal farm turned wildlife reserve · Riyadh
sites.te: A farm that became a wilderness
sites.se: King Khalid's farm north-east of Riyadh, a public park from 1983 and a royal reserve since 2019 where oryx and gazelle are released

sites.desc: A reserve of about 720 km² in the Thumamah area north-east of Riyadh, beside King Khalid International Airport and some 80 km from downtown. It began as King Khalid's private farm; after his death in 1982 it was nationalised, opened as al-Thumamah Wildlife Park on 2 August 1983, and renamed King Khalid Royal Reserve by royal decree in October 2019. Saudipedia records about 195 plant species, 13 mammals, 148 birds and 26 reptiles. On 21 March 2022 the National Center for Wildlife released 20 Arabian oryx and 30 Arabian sand gazelles here, and the King Khalid Wildlife Research Center within the reserve breeds animals for release.

sites.se: Six buried lakes in the Nefud record people returning again and again over 400,000 years
sites.sa: ست بحيرات مدفونة في النفود تسجّل عودة البشر مرة بعد مرة على مدى 400 ألف سنة
sites.desc: Discovered in 2013 by the Palaeodeserts Project in the western Nefud: superimposed palaeolake deposits in an interdunal depression covering about 117,000 m² (700 × 200 m). sites.s: Hail geopark of a giant ancient caldera and young maar volcanoes · UNESCO 2025
sites.dr: UNESCO Global Geopark 2025; managed by NCVC
sites.te: Where a super-volcano met young craters
sites.ta: حيث يلتقي بركان عملاق قديم بفوهات فتيّة
sites.se: Around the Salma Mountains in Hail, the rocks of an ancient giant caldera sit beside dozens of much younger volcanic craters
sites.sa: حول جبال سلمى في حائل تجاور صخورُ كالديرا عملاقة قديمة عشراتِ الفوهات البركانية الأحدث عمرًا بكثير
sites.desc: A geopark of 3,145 km² about 80 km south-east of Hail, joined to the UNESCO Global Geoparks Network in April 2025 and managed by the National Center for Vegetation Cover Development and Combating Desertification. Its core is the Neoproterozoic Salma mega-caldera and batholith, where the Jabal Salma pluton is dated to about 580 Ma and Arabian Shield granite at the western border to about 740 Ma; Salma Mountain rises to 1,380 m. The Pleistocene Hutaymah volcanic field, less than 2 million years old, covers about 900 km² with 77 volcanoes and 119 vent sites, and one of its maars gave an Ar–Ar age of 1.8 ± 0.5 Ma. The park’s geosite material identifies 30 geosites, alongside heritage such as the medieval town of Faid and the Darb Zubaydah pilgrim route.
sites.sig: Brings together one of Arabia’s largest ancient caldera systems and a young maar field in a single protected landscape.

sites.desc: A geopark of about 3,221 km² in Thadiq Governorate, around 140 km north-west of Riyadh, joined to the UNESCO Global Geoparks Network in April 2025 and managed by the National Center for Vegetation Cover Development and Combating Desertification. Its Jurassic and Cretaceous rocks were laid down in the shallow Tethys Ocean and are described as equivalent to some of the largest subsurface oil reservoirs in Saudi Arabia, with Quaternary sand dunes and sabkhas above. Slopes of 20 to 40% form an extension of the Tuwaiq Mountain range, cut by canyons, valleys and terraces, with caves and fossil coral reefs. Listed sites include Table Mountain, Khashm Al-Hussan (the highest point), Ghar Al-Amir, Aba Al-Salabikh cave and the Maghatyah seasonal waterfall.
sites.sig: A field classroom for the marine rock layers that hold Saudi Arabia’s oil, exposed along the Tuwaiq escarpment.

sites.desc: A maar crater in the Pleistocene Hutaymah volcanic field east of the Salma Mountains in Hail, about 1.5 km wide and more than 200 m deep. The maar cut through an earlier scoria cone and lava field, recording a change from magmatic to explosive phreatomagmatic eruptions as magma met groundwater. Salma Geopark describes it as a global reference site for monogenetic volcanism. The Hutaymah field is less than 2 million years old and contains 77 volcanoes and 119 vent sites.
sites.sig: One of the clearest examples in Arabia of a maar volcano formed by magma–water explosions.

sites.s: Maar inside the Salma mega-caldera with mantle rocks and a 1.5 km base-surge section
sites.dr: About 1 Ma (inferred); geosite of Salma UNESCO Global Geopark (2025)
sites.el: Base-surge succession about 1.5 km long and 30 m thick
sites.te: Pieces of the deep Earth
sites.se: Repeated steam explosions here hurled up rocks from the Earth’s mantle and stacked thick ash layers inside an ancient caldera
sites.sa: قذفت الانفجارات البخارية المتكررة هنا صخورًا من وشاح الأرض، وكدّست طبقات رماد سميكة داخل كالديرا قديمة
sites.desc: A maar of the Pleistocene Hutaymah volcanic field that erupted inside an intra-mountain basin of the resurgent granophyre rocks of the Salma mega-caldera in Hail. It records repeated maar formation along fissures in a complex monogenetic system, and phreatomagmatic explosions carried mantle xenoliths to the surface. Its exposed base-surge succession is about 1.5 km long and 30 m thick, described by Salma Geopark as one of the best in the world. Németh (2026) infers an age of about 1 million years.
sites.sig: A rare exposure of base-surge deposits and mantle fragments that shows how maar volcanoes interact with rugged mountain terrain.

sites.s: Wide sediment-filled maar with mantle rocks, and the old village on its rim · Salma Geopark geosites
sites.dr: Formed more than a million years ago; three geosites of Salma UNESCO Global Geopark (2025)
sites.el: Village of about 5,000 people about 90 km south-east of Hail
sites.te: The village on the volcano’s rim
sites.se: Tabah village sits on the rim of a wide old volcanic crater whose floor is slowly sinking
sites.sa: تقع قرية طابة على حافة فوهة بركانية قديمة واسعة، يهبط قاعها ببطء
sites.desc: A wide, relatively flat maar of the Hutaymah volcanic field near the Salma Mountains, partly filled with sediment and ringed by a continuous tuff ring, with visible subsidence of the crater floor. Salma Geopark lists it as a global reference site for mantle xenoliths, and a separate geosite shows the remains of a pre-maar scoria cone and basaltic plug rocks. Németh (2026) infers it formed over a million years ago. Tabah village, among the oldest settlements in the Hail region, was built on the crater rim in pre-Islamic times, lies about 90 km south-east of Hail and has about 5,000 inhabitants; the 1983 earthquakes cracked its buildings.
sites.sig: A place where a volcanic crater, mantle rocks and a long-lived village share one landscape.

sites.n: Jabal Qidr historic scoria cone (Harrat Khaybar)
sites.na: المخروط البركاني التاريخي لجبل القدر (حرة خيبر)
sites.s: Youngest eruption of Harrat Khaybar, whose lava reached Bronze Age desert kites · IUGS Geoheritage Site
sites.el: Cone about 400 m high; crater about 200 m deep and 300 m wide
sites.te: The volcano that buried hunters’ traps
sites.se: Jabal Qidr is the youngest volcano of Harrat Khaybar, and its black lava flowed over ancient desert kites
sites.sa: جبل القدر أحدث براكين حرة خيبر، وقد زحفت حممه السوداء فوق مصائد الصحراء القديمة
sites.desc: A large scoria cone in Harrat Khaybar rising about 400 m above its surroundings, with a crater about 200 m deep and 300 m wide. It is the youngest eruption in the largest intracontinental bimodal volcanic field of the Arabian Peninsula and lies on a roughly north–south fissure that fed tube-fed pahoehoe lava flows. The eruption reached sub-Plinian to violent Strombolian intensity, spreading an ash plain at least 20 km from the vent, and its lava flows reached Bronze Age desert kites. It was named one of the IUGS First 100 Geological Heritage Sites in 2022.
sites.sig: A globally recognised record of young explosive basalt volcanism that overlapped with human occupation of Arabia.

sites.s: Saudi Arabia’s first national park, from Red Sea mangroves to juniper peaks at 3,200 m
sites.el: 6,490.7 km², from sea level to 3,200 m

sites.se: A huge park that climbs from coastal mangroves through acacia woodland to cool juniper forests on the mountain tops
sites.sa: منتزه شاسع يصعد من أشجار القرم على الساحل عبر غابات السَّمُر إلى غابات العرعر الباردة على قمم الجبال
sites.desc: A national park of 6,490.7 km² near Abha in Asir, established in 1981 and spanning elevations from 0 m at the Red Sea coast to 3,200 m on the mountain peaks. The coast receives under 100 mm of rain a year with a mean temperature of about 29 °C, while the highlands receive under 250 mm with about 19 °C. Vegetation runs from mangroves and sparse coastal desert through Acacia woodland and thorn scrub on the western foothills to Juniperus procera woodland above about 1,600 m. sites.desc: A protected area of about 1,540 km² in the canyons north-east of AlUla, managed by the Royal Commission for AlUla since 2019. It protects acacia woodland and native species such as gazelles and the Arabian oryx, and is home to Arabian wolves and Nubian ibex, with restoration central to its management. Sharaan was added to the IUCN Green List in the 2024–2025 listings, assessed against 17 criteria, and was renamed Sharaan National Park; less than 10% of the park is open to motorised tourism.

About 132 native plant species are estimated in the protected area, and wildlife includes Arabian oryx, gazelles, red-necked ostrich and steppe eagles. sites.s: Royal reserve of about 28,000 km² north of Riyadh, split by the Ad Dahna dunes
sites.te: The desert split by a river of sand
sites.se: A huge royal reserve where the red sands of Ad Dahna run between rawdat meadows, escarpments and gravel plains

A vegetation survey recorded 172 plant taxa in 126 genera and 37 families. Four broad habitats were described: seasonally wet pans, wadis, rawdats and floodplains; escarpments and rocky ridges, which held the highest plant diversity; gravel, sandy or rocky plains and plateaux, with the lowest diversity and cover; and the dunes of the Ad Dahna field, which divides the reserve into northern and southern sections. Protected Planet lists it as WDPA 11956 with 28,340 km².
sites.sig: One of the largest protected areas in central Arabia, conserving rawdat wetlands and dune habitats close to the capital.

The area holds coral reefs, mangroves and seagrass beds and is a key habitat for green turtles, dugongs, whales, dolphins and sharks. It is one of three officially listed protected areas in the Makkah region grouped here, with Majami‘ al-Hadb Reserve and the Haram of Makkah.

sites.n: Darb Zubaydah – Al-Neqrah and Al-Jafniyah Pool

sites.desc: A component of the Darb Zubaydah, the pilgrimage road of roughly 1,300 km that linked Kufa with Makkah in the Abbasid period, with stations, water systems and road works. The UNESCO text places Ma‘dan An-Neqrah in a flat agricultural area north of the mountain known as Jabal Ma‘dan. It links the site with ancient copper mining and with pilgrimage facilities, including the Al-Jafniyah Pool. It is one of nine Saudi components of a transnational nomination shared with Iraq.

sites.n: Asiri Highland Landscape: Tihan and Rabea Rufaida
sites.na: المشهد الريفي في مرتفعات عسير: تهان وربع رفيدة

sites.el: Zabnah village lies 12 km north of Borj Tihan
sites.te: Fields stepped across the mountain top
sites.se: In the Asir highlands, low terraces, a watchtower and the old village of Zabnah show how families farmed the mountains
sites.sa: في مرتفعات عسير تروي المدرجات المنخفضة وبرج المراقبة وقرية زبنة القديمة كيف زرع الأهالي الجبال
sites.desc: One of seven elements of the Rural Cultural Landscapes of Sarawat Mountains, a serial nomination in the Makkah, Al-Baha and Asir regions submitted under criteria (ii), (iii) and (v). The fields are low and smoothly terraced and crossed by many wadis. Borj Tihan, in the south of the zone, overlooks the agricultural plateau and the descent to the escarpment. Zabnah, the most significant and best-preserved village, lies 12 km north of the tower and has narrow alleys, gates, an ancient mosque, castles and traditional houses.

sites.s: Ancient Fadak, a palm oasis ringed by a lava-stone wall with 18 towers
sites.dr: UNESCO Tentative List 2022 (Ancient Walled Oases of Northern Arabia, ref. 6575)
sites.el: Wall about 6,800 m long and 2 m high
sites.te: The palm oasis inside a black wall
sites.se: Old Fadak hid its springs and 20,000 palms behind a long wall of black volcanic stone
sites.sa: أخفت فدك القديمة عيونها ونخيلها العشرين ألفًا خلف سور طويل من الحجر البركاني الأسود
sites.desc: Al-Ha’it, known in antiquity as Fadak, is a heritage village in Al-Ha’it Governorate about 250 km south-west of Ha’il city. Its history is traced to before 1200 BC, and the Babylonian king Nabonidus conquered it in 553 BC during his stay in Tayma. A defensive wall of volcanic stone about 2 m high and 6,800 m long, with eighteen square towers and several gates, was built in two phases (1834–1847 and after 1909); only its foundation survives. The oasis was known for about twenty thousand palms fed by springs, and the area has rock art, Thamudic inscriptions and a cuneiform inscription of about twenty-six lines.
sites.sig: One of the walled oases of north-west Arabia, a long-lived settlement model in the desert.

sites.s: Granite domes of Ha’il sheltering the richest wildlife of the arid Arabian interior
sites.dr: UNESCO Tentative List 2023 (Bioclimatic Refugia of Western Arabia, ref. 6638)

sites.desc: A component of the Bioclimatic Refugia of Western Arabia, a natural serial nomination of seven mountain refugia submitted under criteria (vii), (ix) and (x). Jabal Aja is a cluster of pinkish granite domes and pinnacles with ephemeral springs, seeps and Acacia gerrardii woodlands, described as the greatest concentration of biodiversity in the arid interior of the Arabian Peninsula and a Pleistocene refuge. Two taxa are endemic to the site, the grass Trisetaria chaudharyana and the wallflower Erysimum hedgeanum, and relict fauna include griffon vulture, caracal, rock hyrax and Nubian ibex. Wadi Lajb is a deep canyon with the Kingdom’s most important patches of Arabian valley forest and a perennial stream with endemic freshwater fish such as Garra sahilia and Garra tibanica. Al-Jabal al-Aswad in the south-east reaches 2,497 m and carries a cloud forest of African juniper (Juniperus procera), while dense dawm palm woodlands grow on a granite pluton in the south-west. Site endemics include Peucedanum inaccessum, Huernia laevis and Aloe × qaharensis; it is an Important Bird Area.

sites.desc: A component of the Bioclimatic Refugia of Western Arabia, formed of reddish granite crags and pinnacles with Phoenician juniper woodlands, dragon trees, aloes and plants of Mediterranean origin. A Pterocephalus species new to science (aff. sanctus) is endemic to the site, and Arabian endemics include Acacia johnwoodii, Aloe porphyrostachys and Teucrium hijazicum. Relict taxa include the Nubian dragon tree (Dracaena ombet) and Origanum syriacum, and the mountain hosts Nubian ibex, idmi gazelle and possibly the Arabian leopard. Its northern and western parts fall within the Red Sea Project area.

sites.desc: A component of the Egyptian Hajj Road, which linked Egypt with Makkah and Madinah and was used by pilgrims from Egypt, Sudan, Central Africa, Morocco, Andalusia and Sicily. The route had wells, forts, markets and inscriptions and declined as sea travel replaced it, especially after the Suez Canal opened. sites.desc: A component of Prehistoric Stone Structures in Saudi Arabia, a serial nomination of 10 components for which a preliminary estimate gives about 1 million stone structures. Harrat Khaybar is a lava plateau of about 12,000 km² with desert kites of various shapes, wheels, cairns, pendants and mustatils, notably near Samhah. Density is highest near the oases of Khaybar and Al-Ha’it, and a 2014 survey identified 917 kites; barbed kites are exclusive to Khaybar. The plateau, with its volcanoes and lava caves, is also being proposed as a UNESCO Global Geopark.

Stations included That Al-Hajj, Tabuk, Al-Akhdhar, Al-Mu’azam, Al-Hijr and Al-Ula, with pools, tanks, canals, forts, mosques, bridges and markets along the way. Forts on the route stored food for the return journey and sheltered the poor, the lost and those left behind through illness or injury. sites.desc: One of five dams in the Tentative List entry Water Management in Saudi Arabia: The Ancient Dams. The dam lies between two mountains in Wadi Thumalah, about 30 km south-west of Taif. sites.n: Jabal Batharah and Wadi Turabah bioclimatic refugium
sites.s: Granite spires and a perennial stream over 20 km long with three endemic fish
sites.dr: UNESCO Tentative List 2023 (Bioclimatic Refugia of Western Arabia, ref. 6638)
sites.el: Perennial stream flowing more than 20 km
sites.te: The mountain stream that never stops
sites.se: Below grey granite spires, the Wadi Turabah stream flows all year, home to fish and frogs found only in Arabia
sites.sa: تحت قمم الجرانيت الرمادية يجري جدول وادي تربة طوال العام، موطنًا لأسماك وضفادع لا توجد إلا في الجزيرة العربية
sites.desc: A component of the Bioclimatic Refugia of Western Arabia, with grey granite spires, domes and buttresses, montane meadows, tree heather thickets and woodlands of African juniper, wild olive and Acacia origena. On the east side the perennial Wadi Turabah stream flows for more than 20 km through parallel metamorphic ridges and valleys. It is described as one of the richest streams in the Kingdom, with three endemic freshwater fish (Carasobarbus apoensis, Cyprinion mhalensis and Garra buettikeri) and endemic and relict frogs and toads. The site is an Important Bird Area, with species such as Philby’s partridge and the buff-breasted wheatear.

sites.desc: The first element of the Rural Cultural Landscapes of Sarawat Mountains, at the abandoned village of Kherfi in the governorate of Maysan, south of Taif. The apiaries are probably about 500 years old and were passed down within one family; the ensemble could hold 1,300 beehives on different levels. Built of solid stone with stone columns supporting the upper floors, the hives line curved terraces cut into a steep mountainside, terraces made for beekeeping as well as farming. A 20 m high stone fortress overlooks the apiaries, and the site also has agricultural terraces, livestock areas and village ruins.

sites.desc: Magha’ir Shu’ayb in Al-Bad’ Governorate, Tabuk Province, about 225 km from Tabuk city, is the first listed component of the Egyptian Hajj Road. The site was used for burial and housing by the Nabataeans and earlier by the Midianites, and the region’s prosperity is dated to 100 BC–AD 550. The UNESCO text links the place with the Prophet Shu’ayb and describes it as a pilgrim stop with water and pools.

sites.s: Young lava field of scoria cones, maars and white domes · home of Al Wahbah
sites.dr: Mostly Pleistocene; youngest cones younger than about 6,500–4,000 years ago
sites.te: A field of 180 volcanoes
sites.se: Around Al Wahbah lies a whole field of about 180 young volcanoes, some so fresh they erupted after the last green period of Arabia

sites.desc: Harrat Kishb is a volcanic field of about 5,900 km² in Makkah Province, with basaltic scoria cones, tuff rings and maars, and phonolitic lava domes and flows. Most of the field is Pleistocene; Holocene flows are limited to three areas in its western half, and the youngest products (Jabal Aslaj, Jabal Hil and Jabal Shalman) post-date a pluvial period of roughly 6,500–4,000 years ago. Jabal Hil is a large scoria cone whose 300 m wide crater was filled and overtopped by a lava lake, and its pahoehoe flow contains a lava tube up to 20 m wide. Kaminski & Garrison count about 180 volcanoes younger than two million years over roughly 60 × 90 km, including the Al Wahbah maar.
sites.sig: The volcanic setting of the Al Wahbah crater and one of the youngest lava fields of western Arabia.

sites.dr: Jalamid Formation, Turayf Group; mining since 2010
sites.te: Fertiliser from an ancient sea

sites.desc: The Al-Jalamid phosphate mining area lies in the Hazm Al-Jalamid quadrangle (31°–32°N, 39°–40°30′E) in northern Saudi Arabia, where the Jalamid Formation of the early Tertiary Turayf Group consists mostly of pelletal phosphorite, dolomitic limestone and limestone deposited in a shallow sea. Alhawsawi et al. state that the phosphate formed from organic remains roughly 60–70 million years ago; raw ore contains about 20–25% P2O5 and mining began in 2010. In the Sirhan–Turayf basin the Thaniyat Phosphorite Member at the base of the Jalamid Formation is Late Cretaceous, with calcareous phosphorite averaging about 32% P2O5.

sites.desc: Around Dumat al-Jandal the Qasr Member of the Jauf Formation, about 20 m of limestone of late Pragian to early Emsian age (about 405 Ma), contains microbial patch reefs. Individual reefs are circular to elliptical, 1–6 m high and up to 15 m across, while composite buildups reach about 10 m high and 60 m across; their cortices are stromatolites, thrombolites and leiolites, and they lack identifiable metazoan builders. At this locality, about 4 km north-west of Marid Castle, an escarpment exposes numerous bioherms, one of them about 25 m across. The wider Jauf Formation, about 287 m thick, also yields fish remains and fragments of the giant Devonian organism Prototaxites.

sites.te: The sea that came back at the end of the greenhouse
sites.ta: البحر الذي عاد في نهاية العصر الدافئ
sites.se: East of Al-Qurayyat, a cliff of limestone holds tiny fossils from the moment Earth slid from a hot world into a cooler one

sites.desc: The Qurayyat Formation was formally named in 2026 from sections in the Rashrashiyah area east of Al-Qurayyat, with its type section (Rash3) on a southern cliff near the quarry region. It is a Lower Oligocene marine limestone 15–26 m thick (about 26 m at the type section), resting with an erosional disconformity on the Middle–Upper Eocene Rashrashiyah Formation. The disconformity coincides with the extinction of the nannofossils Discoaster saipanensis and D. barbadiensis, and the study recorded 85 nannofossil species in 26 genera. The authors place the Eocene–Oligocene boundary at 33.9 Ma and infer a hiatus spanning part of zones NP19/20 and NP21.

sites.s: Southernmost young volcanic field of Saudi Arabia · erupted about 1810

sites.desc: Jabal Yar is a small olivine-basalt volcanic field on the Red Sea coast at the south-western tip of Saudi Arabia, described by the Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program as the southernmost young volcanic field in the country. It has three volcano groups, Qummatain, Djar’atain-Harra and ‘Ukwatain, and its highest point is 305 m. Hot springs occur south of Djar’atain and between Djar’atain and ‘Ukwatain. Its only recorded eruption, a small explosive eruption (VEI 2) with lava flows, is dated to 1810 ± 10 CE.

sites.desc: Jabal Fayfa is an isolated, steep-sided mountain on the western side of the Asir mountains in Jazan Province, part of the Sarawat range. The Key Biodiversity Area covers about 122 km² between 500 and 2,000 m; its temperate summit is heavily built up and cultivated, and agricultural terraces on the slopes grow coffee and maize. The western slopes receive considerable rainfall, while juniper grows on slopes too steep to terrace. Saudipedia gives an elevation of 1,814 m for the mountain, about 100 km from Jazan city.

sites.te: Where the guineafowl live
sites.se: East of Abu Arish, a green wadi with a small lake is the best place in Saudi Arabia for African birds such as the helmeted guineafowl
sites.sa: شرق أبو عريش يُعد وادٍ أخضر فيه بحيرة صغيرة أفضل مكان في السعودية لطيور أفريقية مثل دجاج الوادي المُخوذ
sites.desc: Wadi Jawwah is a sandy and clay wadi bed between steep volcanic slopes in the foothills east of Abu Arish, inland from Jizan, covering about 63.9 km² at 180–450 m. A small dam holds a lake for most of the year, and vegetation includes Dobera and Ficus trees with Acacia and Salvadora scrub. It is the most important site in Saudi Arabia for the helmeted guineafowl (Numida meleagris), with about 350 birds in 1988 and more than 1,000 in 1990, and has some of the country’s highest densities of breeding Afrotropical birds such as the bateleur. Autumn counts include 975 steppe buzzards and 650 steppe eagles on passage.

sites.desc: Mundafan is a former lake on the south-western edge of the Rub’ al-Khali in Najran Province, occupying a wind-deflated basin of about 363 km² with up to about 24 m of sediment. High stands are dated to Marine Isotope Stage 5 (about 100,000 and 80,000 years ago) and to the early Holocene (about 9,000–6,000 years ago); at its maximum the lake covered about 300 km² and was about 30 m deep. Mussels, snails and stoneworts lived in the water, and aurochs, camels, gazelles, hippopotamuses and ostriches lived around it. Middle Palaeolithic and Neolithic sites around the old shorelines show repeated human occupation.

sites.desc: Harrat al-Birk, west of Abha, is the only Saudi volcanic field lying directly on the Red Sea coast and covers about 1,800 km², separating two coastal plains. Around 200 scoria cones have been identified; volcanism began in the Miocene and continued into the Holocene, and its Quaternary basalt to trachybasalt flows carry ultramafic inclusions. Németh counts 160 vents, eight of them phreatomagmatic, including Surtseyan-style tuff cones near the coast and a maar–tuff ring along Wadi Sabya. Freshly eroded ash around a vent at Jabal Ba’a suggests an eruption within the last century.

The site has one of the few permanent waterfalls in Saudi Arabia, with a pool. The Key Biodiversity Area of about 68.3 km² supports the isolated endemic Asir magpie (Pica pica asirensis) and frogs and toads that depend on permanent water. It is fully included in the protected-area system plan but faces grazing, drainage and visitor pressure.

sites.desc: Safaniya lies offshore in the Arabian Gulf about 225 km north of Dhahran, in water averaging about 22 m deep, and Aramco describes it as the world’s largest conventional offshore oil field. The structure was mapped as a ‘possible high area offshore’ in 1939, and the first offshore well, Safaniyah No. 1, was completed on 15 August 1951. Production began in April 1957 at about 50,000 barrels per day and passed 600,000 barrels per day in 1965. The field measures about 50 × 15 km, its main reservoir is the Cretaceous Safaniya sandstone of the Wasia Formation, and remaining oil was estimated at about 37 billion barrels (2019).

sites.s: Mainland beach north of Yanbu · the best-known green turtle rookery in Saudi Arabia

sites.se: North of Yanbu, hundreds of green turtles crawl ashore each year to lay their eggs, and their numbers have grown since the 1980s

sites.desc: A mainland nesting beach on the Red Sea coast about 70 km north of Yanbu, next to the Yanbu Cement Factory. Annual counts of nesting green turtles (Chelonia mydas) rose from 14–110 females in 1982–1995 to 178 in 2018 and 330 in 2019, and Shimada et al. (2021) estimated an upward trend at the site. Satellite tracking in September–October 2019 (with tagged turtles from Mashabah Island) gave a mean re-nesting interval of 10.8 days and showed nesting success above 0.8 when daytime sand-surface temperature was below 37 °C, falling below 0.4 above 47 °C.
