The island lies within the Al-Wajh Bank area but is about 35 km west of the existing Al Wajh Lagoon pin and is a distinct turtle rookery. Arabic name is a careful transliteration. Region set to Tabuk (Al Wajh governorate).

sites.s: Mangrove lagoon near Duba · close to the northern limit of mangroves on the Saudi Red Sea coast
sites.dr: Northern limit mapped in the KSLOF Atlas (2012)
sites.el: Northern limit of Avicennia marina near 27°25′N
sites.te: The last mangroves of the north
sites.se: Near Duba grow the most northerly grey mangroves on the Saudi Red Sea coast, where the sea becomes too cool and salty for most
sites.sa: قرب ضباء تنمو أشجار القرم الرمادي الأبعد شمالًا على ساحل البحر الأحمر السعودي
sites.desc: The Khaled bin Sultan Living Oceans Foundation Atlas of Saudi Arabian Red Sea Marine Habitats gives Sharm Zubeir (27°25′N), between Al-Sourah and Sharma just north of Duba, as the northern limit of grey mangrove (Avicennia marina) on the Saudi coast. Al-Hasawi (2022) sampled mangrove trees and sediments at a Duba site at 27°25′38″N, 35°36′06″E, described as an inland lagoon away from human activities, as the northernmost of ten stations between Duba and Al-Birk. The same study cites an estimate of about 135 km² of mangrove forest along the Saudi Red Sea shoreline.
sites.sig: Marks the northern edge of mangrove growth on the Saudi Red Sea coast, a natural limit set by climate.
disc: Northern limit of grey mangrove near 27°25′N
About 135 km² of mangroves on the Saudi Red Sea coast
refs: Bruckner, A., Rowlands, G., Riegl, B., Purkis, S., Williams, A. & Renaud, P. (2012). Khaled bin Sultan Living Oceans Foundation Atlas of Saudi Arabian Red Sea Marine Habitats. Panoramic Press, Phoenix, AZ. ISBN 978-0-9835611-1-8. https://livingoceansfoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/01/Red-Sea-Atlas-English.pdf

Al-Hasawi, Z.M. (2022). Determination of potentially toxic metals in mangrove trees and associated sediments along Saudi Red Sea coast. Egyptian Journal of Aquatic Biology & Fisheries 26(6), 595–617. https://ejabf.journals.ekb.eg/article_274585_340cbb9e25600b769fbc9803d5aa7666.pdf
sites.conf: Coordinates are the Duba mangrove station of Al-Hasawi (2022), converted from degrees-minutes-seconds. That station's latitude matches the Atlas's Sharm Zubeir limit (27°25′N), but neither source explicitly says they are the same stand, so the record is named for Duba. The 135 km² figure is Al-Hasawi's citation of Almahasheer et al. (2016). Timeline starts at the Atlas (2012). Arabic name is descriptive.

sites.s: Island-sheltered bay near Al-Lith · densest Sooty Falcon population in Saudi Arabia
sites.te: The bay of the Sooty Falcons
sites.se: A shallow bay hidden behind a long island, where mangrove islets shelter falcons, terns and nesting sea turtles
sites.sa: خليج ضحل يحتمي خلف جزيرة طويلة، تؤوي جُزُره المكسوّة بالقرم الصقور والخطاطيف والسلاحف البحرية التي تعشّش فيه
sites.desc: A shallow bay of about 15 × 35 km on the Red Sea coast near Al-Lith, almost enclosed by a long, narrow island and eight smaller islets, where the Asir mountains come close to the sea. Most islets are fringed by Avicennia mangroves and covered in dense Salicornia, and seagrass beds grow in the bay. The site holds the densest Sooty Falcon (Falco concolor) population in Saudi Arabia, at least 50 breeding pairs of Bridled Tern, and breeding hawksbill and green turtles; dugongs also occur. Traditional trapping of migrating falcons between mid-September and mid-November is listed as a threat.
sites.sig: A key Red Sea site for breeding falcons, seabirds and sea turtles and a bottleneck for migrating raptors.
disc: Densest Sooty Falcon population in Saudi Arabia
At least 50 pairs of Bridled Tern
Hawksbill and green turtles breed here
refs: Key Biodiversity Areas Partnership. Qishran Bay (KBA 8277), Saudi Arabia – site factsheet (BirdLife International data; last assessed 1994). https://www.keybiodiversityareas.org/site/factsheet/8277
sites.conf: Coordinates are the KBA central point; the site covers 586 km², so the pin shows only its general position. Timeline starts from the KBA’s last assessment (1994). Arabic name is a careful transliteration. Region set to Makkah (Al-Lith governorate) from the location.

sites.s: Four small islands off Al-Lith · the largest recorded sea turtle nesting site in Saudi waters
sites.dr: Announced as the largest turtle nesting site, November 2024
sites.te: Four sisters full of turtle nests
sites.se: Far out on the Farasan Banks, four little islands hold more than 2,500 nests of green and hawksbill turtles
sites.sa: في عرض ضفاف فرسان، تحتضن أربع جزر صغيرة أكثر من 2,500 عش للسلاحف الخضراء وصقرية المنقار
sites.desc: Marmar, Dahreb, Malathu and Jadir are four small islands of the Farasan Banks, about 50 km off Al-Lith, lying within about 7 km of Jadir. In November 2024 the General Organization for the Conservation of Coral Reefs and Marine Turtles in the Red Sea (SHAMS) announced that more than 2,500 turtle nests had been recorded there, the largest recorded sea turtle nesting site in Saudi waters. Both green turtles and critically endangered hawksbills nest on the islands. Satellite tags fitted to green turtles on Jadir in 2021 recorded further nesting attempts, most of them on Jadir itself.
sites.sig: The largest documented sea turtle nesting site in the Saudi Red Sea, important for both green and hawksbill turtles.
disc: Green and hawksbill turtles both nest
refs: Tanabe, L.K., Cochran, J.E.M. & Berumen, M.L. (2023). Inter-nesting, migration, and foraging behaviors of green turtles (Chelonia mydas) in the central-southern Red Sea. Scientific Reports 13, 11222. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-37942-z

Scott et al. (2022). Newly described nesting sites of the green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas) and the hawksbill sea turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata) in the central Red Sea. PeerJ 10, e13408. https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.13408
Arab News (2 November 2024). Saudi foundation discovers largest recorded sea turtle nesting site in Red Sea. https://www.arabnews.pk/node/2577799
sites.conf: Pin is Jadir Island, the coordinate published by Tanabe et al. (2023); Scott et al. (2022) give Mar Mar at 19.83576°N, 39.92635°E. The 7 km spacing is from the Tanabe et al. text (their figure caption says 10 km). The nest total is a press-release figure and has not been seen in a peer-reviewed table. Arabic name «جزر الأخوات الأربع» is a translation of the English name. Region set to Makkah (offshore of Al-Lith).

sites.s: Narrow intertidal mudflat in Jazan city · over 20,000 wintering waterbirds counted
sites.te: A city shore full of birds
sites.se: Right beside Jazan city, a thin strip of tidal mud feeds thousands of wading birds in winter
sites.sa: بجوار مدينة جازان مباشرة، يُطعم شريط رفيع من الطين المدّي آلاف الطيور الخوّاضة في الشتاء
sites.desc: A narrow strip of intertidal mudflats about 4 km long and 500 m wide, running from Jizan Port to the northern edge of Jizan city. Sewage outflow from the city enriches the flats, which were once fringed by mangroves that have since been lost to land reclamation. Counts reached 20,053 waterbirds in January 1992, an unusually cold winter, and 10,000–15,000 in December 1992. Part of the site was proposed as a Special Nature Reserve in the NCWCD System Plan for Protected Areas.
sites.sig: Shows how a small urban mudflat can support internationally important numbers of waterbirds.
disc: About 4 km long and 500 m wide
refs: Key Biodiversity Areas Partnership. Jizan Bay (KBA 8289), Saudi Arabia – site factsheet (BirdLife International data; last assessed 1994). https://www.keybiodiversityareas.org/site/factsheet/8289
sites.conf: Coordinates are the KBA central point. Waterbird counts date from 1992 and may not reflect present numbers. Timeline starts from the KBA’s last assessment (1994).

sites.s: Semi-enclosed bay at Baish, Jazan · mangrove seedlings, seagrass and 29 waterbird species studied
sites.te: Baby mangroves against the sandstorms
sites.ta: شتلات القرم في مواجهة العواصف الرملية
sites.se: In a hot, salty bay at Baish, scientists watched young mangroves fight sandstorms while gulls and plovers fed on the seagrass
sites.sa: في خليج حار شديد الملوحة في بيش، تابع العلماء شتلات القرم وهي تقاوم العواصف الرملية، بينما تتغذّى النوارس والزقزاق بين الأعشاب البحرية
sites.desc: A semi-enclosed bay at Baish on the southern Saudi Red Sea coast, inside the Jazan City for Primary and Downstream Industries, with grey mangrove (Avicennia marina) and seagrass. Between April and July 2017, 53 mangrove seedlings were tracked across four tidal zones; only three (5.6%) survived, a loss attributed mainly to burial by sandstorms, while seawater reached 35–37 °C and salinity 46.9–53.01. Bird counts at three stations recorded 29 species from 14 families and 514 individuals, led by Common Gull (202) and Kentish Plover (51), with most birds at the station next to the mangroves.
sites.sig: A natural laboratory for how mangroves and seagrass survive extreme heat, salinity and dust at the southern Red Sea.
disc: Only 3 of 53 seedlings survived the summer
refs: Abrogueña, J.B.R., Anton, A., Woo, S.P., Baptista, M., Duarte, C.M., Hussain, S.A., Shoeb, M. & Qurban, M. (2022). The impact of inundation and sandstorms on the growth and survival of the mangrove Avicennia marina seedlings in the southern Red Sea. Scientia Marina 86(3), e041. https://doi.org/10.3989/scimar.05277.041

Abrogueña, J.B.R., Tanita, I., Doyle, A.M., Roje-Busatto, R., Maquirang, J.R.H., Manokaran, S., Imam, K., Al-Johani, T. & Woo, S.P. (2025). Seagrass and mangroves as water-associated bird habitat in the southern Red Sea coasts of Saudi Arabia. Marine Ornithology 53(1), 87–98. https://www.marineornithology.org/PDF/53_1/53_1_87-98.pdf
sites.conf: Coordinates are the site centre published by Abrogueña et al. (2022); the 2025 bird stations lie within about 2 km (17.32019–17.3587°N, 42.30896–42.32896°E). The 2025 paper’s Discussion says 15 species, conflicting with 29 in its Results; 29 is used. Timeline starts at the 2017 fieldwork. Arabic name is descriptive.

sites.s: Shallow seagrass bay on the Arabian Gulf · about 58,000 wintering waterbirds and feeding dugongs and turtles
sites.te: The seagrass meadow of the Gulf
sites.se: A clear, shallow bay where seagrass feeds dugongs and green turtles and tens of thousands of birds spend the winter
sites.sa: خليج صافٍ ضحل تغذّي أعشابه البحرية الأطوم والسلاحف الخضراء، ويقضي فيه عشرات الآلاف من الطيور فصل الشتاء
sites.desc: A clear, shallow bay on the Saudi coast of the Arabian Gulf around Tarut Island, with mostly sandy bottoms and extensive seagrass beds. Its intertidal zone is among the richest in the Saudi sector of the Arabian Gulf, with broad sand-mud and mud flats once fringed by mangrove and saltmarsh, much of which has been lost to land reclamation. About 58,000 waterbirds wintered here in 1991/92 and more than 20,000 were present in April–May 1991, with six wintering Greater Spotted Eagles and 11 Ospreys. The bay is an important feeding area for green turtles, supports dugongs and serves as a nursery for shrimp and fish.
sites.sig: One of the most productive seagrass and mudflat systems on the Saudi Arabian Gulf coast.
disc: Feeding ground for green turtles and dugongs
refs: Key Biodiversity Areas Partnership. Tarut Bay (KBA 8262), Saudi Arabia – site factsheet (BirdLife International data; last assessed 1994). https://www.keybiodiversityareas.org/site/factsheet/8262
sites.conf: Coordinates are the KBA central point; it lies about 4 km from the existing Tarout Island (archaeological) pin but records the bay’s ecology, not the island’s archaeology. Bird counts date from 1991–1992. Timeline starts from the KBA’s last assessment (1994).

sites.s: Isolated mountain west of Bisha · proposed Important Plant Area with endemic aloe and dragon trees
sites.te: The lonely mountain of rare plants
sites.se: A lone mountain west of Bisha shelters 118 kinds of plants, including an aloe found only in Saudi Arabia and a few rare dragon trees
sites.sa: جبل منعزل غرب بيشة يحتضن 118 نوعًا من النباتات، منها صبر لا ينمو إلا في السعودية وأشجار دم الأخوين النادرة
sites.desc: Jandaf Mountain is an isolated mountain in the Asir region about 60 km west of Bisha, rising to a summit of 1,910 m above the surrounding Wadi Tarj. A survey in late March 2018 covering about 30 km² recorded 118 plant species in 97 genera and 42 families, mostly perennials. Notable taxa include the national endemic Aloe pseudorubroviolacea, the regional endemic Monolluma quadrangula and the Endangered Dracaena serrulata, of which only about three individuals were found. Annual precipitation is about 126 mm and mean annual temperature about 25 °C. The authors conclude that the mountain meets Important Plant Area and High Conservation Value Area criteria and recommend strict protection.
sites.sig: A small inland mountain whose plant richness rivals much larger areas of the Bisha region, making it a candidate for strict protection.
refs: Al-Namazi, A.A., Algarni, S.M., Wan, J.S.H., Al Mosallam, M.S. & Alotaibi, F. (2022). Floristic composition of Jandaf Mountain as biodiversity hotspot area in southwestern Saudi Arabia. Saudi Journal of Biological Sciences 29, 3654–3660. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sjbs.2022.03.003
sites.conf: Coordinates read as 19°33′N, 42°20′E from the paper’s text, where the degree and minute symbols are lost (printed ‘19330 N, 42200E’); point is the mountain, not a plot. Arabic name is a careful transliteration

sites.s: Juniper-zone park near Tanomah · nesting site of the endangered Asir (Arabian) magpie
sites.el: 1,950 m; four nests found in June 2016
sites.te: Home of the rare blue-black magpie
sites.se: In a mountain park near Tanomah, one of Arabia’s rarest birds, the Asir magpie, still builds its nests
sites.sa: في منتزه جبلي قرب تنومة ما زال العقعق العسيري، أحد أندر طيور الجزيرة العربية، يبني أعشاشه
sites.desc: Al Mehfar park lies about 5 km north-west of Tanomah at 1,950 m in the Asir highlands, within the juniper forest zone. Babbington (2016) recorded one Asir magpie (Pica pica asirensis) there on 22 January 2014, two birds and a nest on 23 May 2014, four birds including two juveniles in July 2014 and four birds in July 2015. No birds were seen in summer 2016, but four nests, two of them new, were found in June 2016. The taxon lives mainly in upland valleys at 1,850–3,000 m, and its breeding population has been estimated at a minimum of 135 pairs; habitat loss from tourism and development and juniper dieback are the main threats.
sites.sig: One of the few recently confirmed breeding places of a magpie found only in the Asir highlands.
disc: At 1,950 m in the juniper zone
refs: Babbington, J. (2016). Update on the status and occurrence of Arabian Magpie Pica pica asirensis in Saudi Arabia. Sandgrouse 38, 146–151. https://osme.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/Update-on-the-status-and-occurrence-of-Arabian-Magpie-Pica-pica-asirensis-in-Saudi-Arabia.pdf
sites.conf: Coordinates are the published locality point. Arabic park name is a careful transliteration. The population estimate (Jennings 2010) is quoted by Babbington, who thinks the true number is probably lower

sites.s: Rocky slope in Qilwah · largest recorded stand of the endangered endemic Aloe shadensis
sites.te: The aloe of a single valley
sites.se: On dry rocky slopes in Qilwah grows an aloe found almost nowhere else on Earth, and only a few dozen plants were counted
sites.sa: على منحدرات صخرية جافة في قلوة ينمو صبر يكاد لا يوجد في أي مكان آخر على الأرض، ولم يُحصَ منه إلا بضع عشرات من النباتات
sites.desc: A rocky dry slope in Qilwah Governorate, Al-Bahah, at about 578 m, where a 2022 survey counted 20 individuals of Aloe shadensis, an endangered species endemic to Saudi Arabia. The survey (January–September 2022, 400 m² plots) found the species at only a few sites in the Qilwah and Al-Mukhwah governorates, with an area of occupancy of 20 km² and an extent of occurrence of 188 km², both in the endangered range. Mean annual rainfall is 21.7 mm at Qilwah. The aloe is most abundant on rocky dry slopes facing wadis and is threatened by its low density, narrow range and nearby expanding settlements.
sites.sig: A key locality for one of the most narrowly distributed plants of the Al-Bahah foothills.
refs: Al-Khulaidi, A.W.A. & Alzahrani, F.A. (2023). Geographic distribution of endangered endemic species Aloe shadensis Lavranos & Collen. (Asphodelaceae) in Saudi Arabia. Pakistan Journal of Botany 55(6), 2345–2350. http://dx.doi.org/10.30848/PJB2023-6(32)
sites.conf: Coordinates are the published plot point. The altitude column in the source table is garbled; 578 m is taken from the text. Endangered status is the authors’ assessment from range size

sites.n: Hawala and Jabal Uthrub plant hotspot (Baljurashi)
sites.na: بؤرة التنوع النباتي في حوالة وجبل أثرب (بلجرشي)
sites.s: Sarawat slopes south-west of Baljurashi · 319 plant species, juniper the most frequent
sites.te: Juniper slopes full of plants
sites.se: On the misty mountain slopes near Baljurashi, scientists counted 319 kinds of plants, with juniper trees the most common
sites.sa: على منحدرات الجبال الضبابية قرب بلجرشي أحصى العلماء 319 نوعًا من النباتات، وكان العرعر أكثرها انتشارًا
sites.desc: A biodiversity hotspot on the Sarawat Mountains near Baljurashi, south-west Al-Bahah, including Hawala, Jabal Uthrub, Al Abna and Huzna, surveyed between April 2017 and July 2018. Ninety-seven 20 × 20 m plots across 167.6 km² recorded 319 plant species in 228 genera and 75 families, including 2 species endemic to Saudi Arabia, 14 near-endemics and 39 rare or endangered species. Juniperus procera was the most frequent species (49% of plots), and Erica arborea occurred above 2,000 m. The richest plots lay on high-altitude slopes around Hawala and the top of Al Abna.
sites.sig: One of the richest documented plant areas of the Arabian Peninsula’s south-western escarpment.
refs: Al-Namazi, A.A., Al-Khulaidi, A.W.A., Algarni, S. & Al-Sagheer, N.A. (2021). Natural plant species inventory of hotspot areas in Arabian Peninsula: Southwest Al-Baha region, Saudi Arabia. Saudi Journal of Biological Sciences 28(6), 3309–3324. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sjbs.2021.02.076
sites.conf: Coordinates are the centre of the published study bounds (about 19.41–19.50° N, 41.29–41.44° E). The paper gives inconsistent elevation ranges and endemic counts; figures here follow its results tables. Arabic spellings of Hawala and Uthrub are careful transliterations

sites.na: الصوان الحامل للذهب في حفة عابث
sites.s: Folded iron-rich chert in Precambrian Arabian Shield rocks north of Al-Bahah · host of ancient gold workings
sites.el: Workings extend more than 120 m down the hillside
sites.te: Gold hidden in folded stone
sites.se: North of Al-Bahah, ancient miners followed gold through a band of rusty, folded chert squeezed between very old rocks
sites.sa: شمال الباحة تتبّع المعدّنون القدماء الذهب في شريط من الصوان الصدئ المطويّ بين صخور قديمة جدًا
sites.desc: Haffa Abith lies in the southern Wadi Bidah district of the Arabian Shield, in the Jabal Ibrahim and Al Aqiq quadrangles. Gold here occurs in folded ferruginous chert within a Precambrian sequence of carbonaceous schist, carbonate-bearing tuff, dolomitic marble, metabasalt and graywacke, tied to quartz veins, stringers and stockworks. The chert-hosted deposits of the district have low silver and base-metal contents and anomalous arsenic. Ancient open cuts and declines extend more than 120 m down a steep hillside; the site was found by the survey in May 1979.
sites.sig: A clear example of how gold in the Arabian Shield concentrated in iron-rich chert layers of old volcanic-sedimentary basins.
refs: Worl, R.G. & Smith, C.W. (1982). Reconnaissance investigations of ancient gold mines in the southern part of the Wadi Bidah District, Jabal Ibrahim and Al Aqiq quadrangles, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. U.S. Geological Survey Open-File Report 82-789. https://doi.org/10.3133/ofr82789
sites.conf: The source gives only ‘Precambrian’; the timeline uses a broad Neoproterozoic estimate (850–600 Ma). Arabic name is a careful transliteration. Coordinates are from the report text

sites.na: منجم الذهب القديم في بني سار
sites.s: Ancient gold workings along 2.5 km of quartz veins just north of Al-Bahah city
sites.te: The miners’ trench of Bani Sar
sites.se: Near Bani Sar, old miners dug pits, shafts and trenches along gold-bearing quartz veins for more than two and a half kilometres
sites.sa: قرب بني سار حفر المعدّنون القدماء حفرًا وآبارًا وخنادق على امتداد عروق الكوارتز الحاملة للذهب لأكثر من كيلومترين ونصف
sites.desc: The Bani Sar ancient mine lies just north of Al-Bahah city and is one of the few ancient gold mines in the southern Wadi Bidah district that can be reached directly by vehicle. Ancient open cuts, pits and shafts follow a quartz-vein system for more than 2,500 m within a narrow, schistose diorite intrusion about 15 km long. A US Geological Survey team investigated the workings in April 1980 and found the deposit encouraging but in need of more surface work to define its extent. The workings themselves are not dated; archaeological study of Al-Bahah’s mining landscape places Islamic-era mining in the region between the 7th and 12th centuries AD.
sites.sig: Among the most extensive ancient mine workings in the Al-Bahah highlands, linking the region’s rocks to its mining past.
refs: Worl, R.G. & Smith, C.W. (1982). Reconnaissance investigations of ancient gold mines in the southern part of the Wadi Bidah District, Jabal Ibrahim and Al Aqiq quadrangles, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. U.S. Geological Survey Open-File Report 82-789. https://doi.org/10.3133/ofr82789
Al-Zahrani, A.A.A. (2014). Mining in Al-Baha Region, South-Western Saudi Arabia in Islamic-Era: The Archaeology of Asham. PhD thesis, University of York. https://etheses.whiterose.ac.uk/6483/
sites.conf: The Bani Sar workings are undated in the source; the timeline (about AD 600–1150) is a broad estimate from the regional Islamic-era mining dates in Al-Zahrani (2014), not a date for this site. Coordinates are from the USGS report text

sites.s: Permanent river of treated water south of Riyadh · reedbeds and lagoons with over 220 bird species
sites.te: A river in the desert
sites.se: South of Riyadh, treated water keeps a river flowing all year through Wadi Hanifah, drawing herons, eagles and more than 220 kinds of birds
sites.sa: جنوب الرياض تُبقي المياه المعالجة نهرًا جاريًا طوال العام في وادي حنيفة، فيجذب البلشونات والعقبان وأكثر من 220 نوعًا من الطيور
sites.desc: Al-Ha’ir is an artificial, permanently flowing river of treated effluent run-off that runs for about 50 km along Wadi Hanifah, 25 km south of Riyadh, covering a Key Biodiversity Area of 49.8 km² at 480–600 m. The river flows mostly between rocky cliffs, with many pools fringed with reeds and Tamarix, and in places forms wide lagoons between sand dunes beside small pivot-irrigated farms. More than 220 bird species have been recorded, including 20 greater spotted eagles (Aquila clanga) and 17 western marsh harriers (Circus aeruginosus). Little bittern, squacco heron, purple heron and Eurasian reed warbler breed, and black storks winter.
sites.sig: A rare permanent wetland in the arid Najd plateau, important for wintering raptors and breeding herons.
refs: Key Biodiversity Areas Partnership. Al-Ha’ir (KBA 8266) factsheet. https://www.keybiodiversityareas.org/site/factsheet/8266
sites.conf: Coordinates are the KBA central point. Timeline starts from the last assessment (1994); bird counts date from that assessment

sites.s: Desert wadi beside Arar · 196 plant species, mostly annuals after winter rain
sites.te: The wadi that blooms after rain
sites.se: Next to the city of Arar, a dry desert valley bursts into life after winter rain with almost 200 kinds of plants
sites.sa: بجوار مدينة عرعر يدبّ النشاط في وادٍ صحراوي جاف بعد أمطار الشتاء، فتظهر فيه قرابة 200 نوع من النباتات
sites.desc: Wadi Arar is a typical desert wadi of the Northern Borders region next to Arar city, with a hot arid climate, a mean annual temperature of 21.5 °C and about 20.2 mm of rain a year, mostly in winter. Surveys of 25 localities, including its tributaries, between November 2011 and April 2013 recorded 196 plant species in 130 genera and 31 families. Compositae (48 species), Gramineae (26) and Leguminosae (22) were the richest families. Annuals made up 136 species (69.5%) and therophytes 140 species (71.5%), a typical desert spectrum.
sites.sig: A baseline record of the rain-driven desert flora of Saudi Arabia’s far north.
refs: Osman, A.K., Al-Ghamdi, F. & Bawadekji, A. (2014). Floristic diversity and vegetation analysis of Wadi Arar: A typical desert Wadi of the Northern Border region of Saudi Arabia. Saudi Journal of Biological Sciences 21(6), 554–565. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sjbs.2014.02.001
sites.conf: Coordinates are the single study-area point given in the paper. A parallel version (Taeckholmia 34, 2014) gives 194 species; figures here follow the Saudi Journal of Biological Sciences paper. The King Salman Royal Reserve Arar sampling site on the map lies about 7 km away

sites.s: Historic protected rangeland around Faid · 22 reptile species recorded
sites.te: The old protected land of lizards
sites.se: Around the old pilgrim town of Faid, a traditional protected land is home to 17 kinds of lizards and 5 kinds of snakes
sites.sa: حول بلدة فيد القديمة على درب الحجاج يحتضن حمى تقليدي 17 نوعًا من السحالي و5 أنواع من الثعابين
sites.desc: Faid Hema is a historical protected area (hema) of about 4,800 km² around the town of Faid in Ha’il region, about 4.1% of the region’s area; Faid lay on the pilgrimage road between Kufa and Makkah. A survey of five sites from November 2012 to December 2013 recorded 22 reptile species, 17 lizards and 5 snakes, from 134 individuals. Nine species were new records for the hema, and Mesalina adramitana and Walterinnesia aegyptia were first records for Ha’il region. The richest site, Jannin, held about half of all species, while an agricultural site held the fewest; the authors suggest that grazing and hunting control helped keep reptile diversity high.
sites.sig: Shows how a traditional Arabian hema can still conserve desert wildlife.

sites.desc: A station of the Ottoman Hejaz Railway at Al-Hijr (Mada’in Salih), about 1 km north of the main Nabataean area of Hegra in AlUla. Construction of the railway began in 1900, and the line reached Medina on 1 September 1908; the completed Damascus–Medina section was 1,300 km long on a 1,050 mm gauge. The station building has been converted into a hotel, and the engine shed serves as its main restaurant and displays a 2-6-0 Jung locomotive. The Hejaz Railway, including this station, is on Saudi Arabia's UNESCO Tentative List (2015).
